Princess Victoria of Wales, during her stay in town, took things very quietly, keeping early hours, and getting plenty of open air exercisee. But despite every care, the rush of the London season proved too much for her, and she has had to flit off to Cromer again to take the air which has before proved so beneficial to her. There is no disguising the fact that Princess Victoria is in a very delicate state of health, and that she is cans- ing her friends no little anxiety again. although some of our society papers persist in remarking that the Princess is "now enjoying excellent health." About the end of the month, the Princess will accom- pany her mother on a visit to the King and Queen of Denrnark,and among other members of the Danish Royal family gathered at flernatoiff at the same time, will be the King and Queen of Greece, the Duke and Duchess of Cumberland, and their children, and Prince and Princess Carl s,f Sweden. These summer reunions are eagerly looked forward to by the K•ng and Queen of Denmark. Queen Louise is, on these occasiona,her own housekeept r and special attention is paid to the little likings of her children and grandchildren,and their respective partners. During this summer holiday Queen Louise forgets her many town interests and charities, and gives herself up ter the joy of unrestrained intercourse with her many loved ones.

When the happy summer gathering is over, and the King and Queen are once more left comparatively alone Queen Louise devotes a portion of every day to thq many institutions she has started at Copenhagen and other towns. She has a clear, and powerful business head, and her early habits of economy serve her in good stead when organising an orphanage or industrial se.hool. Sufferers and children have always found a faithful friend and helper in the Danish Queen, and her splendid work in this dlrectkn has always had the warm and active . sympathy of her Royal husband. King Christian.

It is the law of Denmark that Christian must be suc- ceeded by Frederick and Frederick by Christian. Den- mark's Kings for more than four hundred years have all been named Christians or Fredericks. Every Danish prince therefore receives these two names among those bestowed upon him at baptism, be his chances nf suc- cession ever so small. Before the second half of the seventeenth century, surnames were unknown among the Danish people, a child simply taking the ehristian name of his or her father. One of Christian Victoria,i arbitrary laws was to alter the state of affairs,by com- pelling2every man to assume some definite family title. Weddings are coming thick and fast row, and when one realises kow much prettier a summer wedding is than a winter specimen, one cannot but marvel that a woman ever cosiest to be married at any other season of the year. The orthodox bridal turnout, is not ono of the warmest and consist of toilettes, and what bride can hepe to look her best if she is pinched with celd. On a warm bright summer day, white satin and chiffon are in accordance with our feelings. Morover, the light airy fairy toilettes possible for bridesmaids and guests, make the Beene an infinitely more fascinating one. The most picturesque wedding of the now closing London season, has been that of Miss Fleetwood Wilber), and Prince Alexie Dolgorouke. The second ceremony took place in the Russian Chapel in Welbeck-street, and this was most magnificent and impressive. The room, in the centre of which stood an altar, covored with a gold cloth, was filled with exquisite white flowers, and priests in gold raireent intoned the prayers, to which an unseen orchestra gave musical responses. The bride and bridegroom on entering were each presented with a lighted candle, and bouquets of orange blossom. After- wards were brought in two wedding tines, which were duly exchanged between the happy pair. Then two gold crowns were held above their heads, and an open gold cup presented, from which both drank three times. Next came a proce-eion round the altar, and when the ceremony was completed the head priest blessed them, and they turned and left the chapel the moat radiant couple imaginable. The Terrace of the House of Commons has been some- what less crowded this season than has been the case in former years, swing partly to the weather, and partly to the new regulations which compel a member to obtain an order if he wishes to introduce his women friends to the Lobby. Still the scene has frequently been a very gay ono, and needless to say the narrow-minded,crabbed variety, may still be heard to erumhle about our beirg allowed on the terrace at all. By the majority however, our presence is appreciated, and on bright gunny after- nonne pretty frocks and faces, have been well to the fore. _

The latest among Royal ladies to have her miniature painted, is the Duchess of York. Her Royal Hiehness has lately teen giving Signor Luigi Bernieri sittings. Signor Bernieri is a Florentine and he has devoted him- self to the study of miniature werk fey years past. He has studied in Rome, Paris, and London, and exhibited in all three cities at various times. Those women whose purses will alio.' of it, are now eschewing the ordinary photograph for miniatures, and doubtless these are wise in doing so. How unrecoenisahle do Rome of us find onrselves and our friends, when translated in'n hard black and white, whereas, in a miniature, the soft- ness of the tint is equal to that of the best cemplexion —Nature's own ! For a miniature though we muet bear in mind the het that a bard or severe toilette is impossible—also flaring enlours. In a miniature one expects something leer d . scisive a kind of vague cloudiness. and also—one expectsbeau.y as well. It it silly to be sure, but the first impulse of the spectator is to resent a plain nr uninteresting face. But if the craze for miniatrree gees on, we shall soon get accustomed to see all sorts of faces, justfas we do in photographs. At this time of year, when the majority of U 9 are upon l ol day thaug,hts intent, we should do well to re• member that confortable boots and shoes are the most important items in our wardrobe. A boot or shoe that hurts or pinches is quite enough to spoil the most g'ori- ous hotiday possible. To be stranded with nothing hut new and unsympathic boots and shees at this particular time, is a sore trial. They really ought Cr. he in our pnspeEsion some weeks before they are likely to he called upon to enter active service, and during this period exercised daily, in the house, for at least half an ' hour. But if you have failed to look ahead, then the i next thing is to buy our footgear amply wide, and long. Better a few unsightly, wrinkles than a el:toiled holiday. According to a well-known man of science, we should I wear cheap boots and shoes, and throw them aside after a short period of service. The foot, he says, as an accumulator nf dirt, and a conservator of perspiration, is bead and shoulders above the whole system, and the disease laden perspiration is absorbed by the leather, until the old shoe becomes a danger to health. The high-priced shoe, owing to the firmer texture of its leather, and its consequently Superior listing qaaltiee, becomes with increasing age, a perfect hot-bed of de- cayed perspiration, with several m llmo germs to the inch'! All this is very startling no doubt. But I ques- tion whether we should gain much by exchangine , quality for quantity, except corm. So far as Wear- since goes we should decidedly be the losers. Personally. if I had to make my choice, I should vote for the mi- crobes, and take my chance. Buff and blue is the combination of the moment for "easiee and country gowns, and a great deal of red too is en evidence again, for boating and seaside frocks. A dainty toilette I inspected a few mornings back, which was just about to he sent off to well-knewn society beauty,was in nun's veiling,of a drab shade. The skirt was plain, with three tucks at the bottom, the jacket bodice tucked all over,sleeves as well. The opera front showed a collar band and cravat of red accerelion pleated chiffon, there was a red silk belt, a red hat, turned back sharply with a huge butterfly bow of black velvet, and trimmed with red tulle. The combination was a delightful one,and the whole creation very fascin- ating to gaze upon. Cold cream may be made as follows :—Take half a pound of the best lard,and a little essence of lemon, rut these in a basin-and pour boiling water upon them.then set aside, and when cold pour off the water. Twice re- peat this process of scalding,then beat with a fork, to a soft cream. Put in jers, and it is ready for use. TEA TWISTS.—Work two ounces of butter (or good beef dripping) into a pound of flour, and a little salt. Beat up two eggs,and mix into the flour, adding enough milk to make a dough. Roll out and cut into strips, plait three in a short roll, brush over with egg,and bake in a sharp oven. I" MADGE.'

THE FIRST 'STEP.—" I wish you would tell me," said the kind old judge to the lady burglar, "how I pu came to adopt such a disreputable profession. ' How did you begin?" "Your honour," replied the miserable woman, "my first step was to go through my husband's pockets while he slept. After that the descent was easy." "Well, I tried two hull days to sell 'im, an' no one offored more'n five shillings, so I went, like a honest man, an' guv him to th' ole lady what owned 'im, and she guy me a suvrin."

BEFORIG TDB BLESSING.—The company were assembled to dinner. The fond mother, wishing sto display the intellectual powers of her little daughter, by getting her to ask a blessing clues- ' tioned her in the following manner—" My little dear, what do you always do before eating your dinner?" "I's pick the flies out of my broth," . promptly replied the little one. CLOSED FOE THE NlGHT.—Parent (at head of stairs): "Clara 1 It's time for you to go to bed." Clara (in the parlour) : "Why, .pa, Mr. Greene is here 1" "Oh, I beg pardon. I thought it was Mr. Brown, and I haven't any patience with Mr. Brown. He always kisses you so noisily that it wakes me up. Stay as long as you please, Mr. Greene, you are always welcome." Mr. Greene: "Urn I—thank you, but I was just getting ready to go, and I—l promised my churn I'd be back early. "Good night?" "I am glad they moved away," remarked the good housewife, speaking of a family of borrowing neighbours who had just left the city. "I was willing to lend them a loaf of bread occasionally, or a half-dozen of eggs, or the washboard, or the • lemon squeezer, but when they got down to send- ing the little girl over to borrow pennies to give the organ-grinder, I began to think it was nearly time to draw the line. And, to cap the climax, one day they actually asked. me to come over and take care of the baby while they went down town !" CLEARING ruin ROAD.—A man, whose nose was an extraordinarily large one, was employed by a road contractor to keep the road clean. One day, whilst scraping the road. Lord C— drove up in a gig, and seeing a man with such a large nose he • pulled up to have a good look at it. The road. man, knowing very well the, cause of the noble- man's surplise, and wishing, perhaps, to remind him of his ba4 manners, took hold of his nose and Ipulled it to the one side, saying at the same time to his Lordship, "You may go past now, sir." Lord C— took the hint, and handing the road. man a crown drove on his way. Mona MORTAR ! "—An Irish labourer was serv- ing a squad of masons, who, when requiring more lime, were in the habit of shouting from the scaffolding, "Lime, Pat!" In a room at the 'foot of the gangway some tailors were at work' who annoyed Pat by imitating the masons, calling "Lime, Pat !" One day he thought he would be even with them, so mixing up a hod of lime very thin he threw it in at the open window where they were sitting with the exclamation, "Shout when ye want more, jintlemen !" How ODD !—Mrs. Simpkins: "Are you fond of music, Mr. Verdi ?" Mr. Verdi (stammering) : "No—yes---that is—l mean—at times." Mrs Simpkins "Indeed, Mr. Verdi? Do you mean that some people can move your musical emotions, and not others?" Mr. Verdi: " Aki, yes, Mrs. Simpkins, that is it—exactly." Mrs. Simpkins: "You are doubtless touched only with the finest performers, Mr. Verdi. You find yourself en- chanted with the playing of a Paderewski, or swayed by the divine melody of a Patti." Mr. Verdi (rising to the occasion) : "No, Mrs. Simp- kins. My musical soul is strange and unique in this—l am roused to emotion only when lam the performer myself. No friend, no acquaintance •ever shares my joy. I exult alone." Mrs. Simpkins' (overpowered): "How very strange !" • A B.,CRAL PROPOSAL. —My solitary attempt at proposing led to such a ludicrous fiasco that I have never felt tempted to make a second attempt. I lad longed for an opportunity to declare my passion. One evening as she and I were strolling round the garden together I th!mght the oppor- tunity had come. Lat at the critical moment my •courage failed me. I could, get no further than: " Lucy--er, Just J as I had said time •4‘ Lucy—er " for about the 10th nue a cow put her head over the low hedge that ran round the garden. In desperation I blurted out: "What f i a i motherly was creature a cow looks I" "Yes, to aea the answer. Only for that cow I might have been happy man to-day- .

div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

- --- M Y DRAB NELLIZ, With regard to millinery there is no especially prevailing shape or style, as was the case some years ago. Bonnets have the trimming set imme- diately in front, over the face. Very pretty is a white chip bonnet, with wide bows of white satin ribbon of a soft rich quality in front, and a hand- some paste ornament in the centre, a full feathery aigrette with black spots starting from behind the buckle; the strings are of white satin. Blue tulle bows and black feathers secured by a jet crescent form the trimming of a black straw bonnet, while a pretty-coloured satin straw is draped with the same coloured striped gauze and has a large bunch of feathery green grasses in the centre.

A very pretty toque is made of black glace silk, which is veiled with transparent black crazy net, on which white chenille spots of different sizes are showered. Lovely shaded pink roses trim the left side, and above them there is a fancy black osprey. A grey shiny-looking straw toque has the upturned brim edged with grey velvet, the bows being of white silk gauze and the grey ostrich feathers spangled with jewels—a fashion gaining ground very rapidly, though not in accordance with Nature, and therefore inartistic and not to be commended. Cream lace, straw, jet, and double pink geraniums combine to make a dainty-looking toque. Another, equally satisfactory, is of white straw, white tulle, pink roses, and black velvet bows.

An alpaca skirt in grey, or a pretty hyacinth. blue and pink is not amiss for wear at the seaside, and looks well with a white blouse and rose- trimmed hat. Then on cool or damp afternoons the serge skirt and Eton coat can be worn, with its sleeveless vest of muslin trimmed cascades of lace, and a.smart belt; and a sleeveless vest of pale fawn cloth, with a little gold braid, or a high one of fawn drill with red spots would be useful, and occupy no room at all in the basket. A fur tie or feather boa can also be put in, as the evenings on the pier are sometimes very cold, and an extra wrap is welcome.

A dress suitable for boating expeditions is made of rather light blue serge; the Eton jacket, cut with rather long pointed fronts and wide revers, opening over a tucked linen vest, with an upper collar of linen hem-stitched round the edge. A yachting or boating gown looks well in tan and white. The material is Berge, and the colour the exact shade of brown yacht-sails. The coat and skirt of the serge, and the leaf-shaped tablier and deep turned-over coat collar of thick white flax, ornamented with veinings in silk stitching, the bordering being of narrow string lace and gold cord. A vest of rose and .white striped satin is worn beneath the coat, with satin belt fastened with a neat silver buckle. White serge, with the coat and skirt seams stitched with blue silk, the closely-set rows of stitching having the effect of a novel sort of braid, makes a neat yachting costume.

The unlined blouse is now made in so many styles that it is quite a distinct garment from the shirt of cotton or flannelette, although the small bishop sleeves are almost identical. Now, presum- ing that you are making a loose, unlined blouse, you would cut it in three parts, of course adding the other front, one only being shown in the diagram. The lines at centre of back and front denote tiny pleats, which give the full effect, sad for the waist there should be a folded band of the material, about one and a-quarter to one and a-half inches wide, and made up to the exact size required, and the seamed-up blouse is then pleated up to the same size, and the band stitched on at the waist, putting the blouse in between the folds of the band. Even if the blouse is made with a shaped or fitted lining, the material is cut in this fashion, but lining may have as few seams as possible. Apropos of the blouse, which is now at last relegated to morning wear, some of the latest are made of the stuff known as mousseline brillante, over white or other coloured taffetas, are all that is of the most charming, with their dainty tucks and insertions and feather stitching generally. A French blouse, while unequivocally extravagant, is quite equally chic and engaging enough to justify it of its cost, and one case in point, a heartrending specimen in green and white silk muslin over ciel blue taffetas, which has cost a beat friend a fort- night's income, really claims indulgence for its wicked price by reason of its undoubted allure- ments. We needs must love the dearest when we see it, as her cynical husband with a gift for paraphrasing remarked; but with a sentiment also so applicable to his own sex I really wonder that he allowed himself the luxury of that misquoted quantity.. Your loving Jissrstiß.

open; there is ott a sup 'twin cup and lip.'" De Retz reified in his horse. "Take Yves with you, Gildas, he said, and rice on to Laval to announce our coming, so that all may be ready to receive Madame la Comtesse:" Gillonne looked keenly at the young leader; s,he Bali' that he was far more attractive than he had. looked when he assisted - at- the marriage in the chapel at Longuedec. It seemed to her that he was more richly dressed; he now wore a spray of rich jewels under the flap of his velvet toquet ; there was, too, a handsome escarelle at his girdle, from which three long golden ornaments dangled beside the hip. She remarked that the pommel of his long dagger was so covered with jewels that they seemed ablaza in the setting sunlight. The sagacious tirewoman asked herself what would happen if the Count of Laval did not recover, and this gorgeous-looking cavalier succeeded as next heir. She lay awake all night harassed with doubts and fears, and next morning, when they set forth on the last stage of their journey, she resumed her place in the litter with her mistress. She had determined to give her lady some inkling of what might lie before her, and she presently told Jeanne that she feared the Count's illness was of a very serious nature. Jeanne felt greatly disturbed. "I pray that it may not be so; but I believe we are to reach Laval to-day."

She hardly spoke again till the cavalcade began to mount the hill on which stood the dark fortress- castle of Laval. Jeanne looked forth from the litter, eager to get a glimpse of her future home. She saw that it was built on the steep hillside, and was partly surrounded by tall gabled dwellings, which bordered the twisting street of the town. The river Mayenne had to be crossed before they could approach the Castle gates, and Jeanne noted with surprise that the bridge was guarded at either end. The blast of a trumpet gave notice of their approach, and the litter was soon going at a quick pace over the Castle drawbridge. Be Retz had preceded her, and he was ready to help her alight when the litter stopped before the frowning portal of Laval.

Behind De Retz stood two grey-bearded men, in one of whom Jeanne recognised the Chamberlain who had accompanied her husband to Longuedec ; the other was evidently the Seneschal, for the Castle keys hung at his girdle. They both made her reverential obeisances ; but as the young Countess looked from one old face to the other their sad expression chilled her heart and filled her with anxiety. "How fares my lord the Count of Laval?" she asked the Seneschal. De Retz took upon himself to answer. "Will Madame la Comtesse be pleased to enter ? " he said. "Her question can then be more fittingly answered." The Chamberlain turned to lead the way, and De Retz walked beside Jeanne. She was oppressed by the gloom of her reception; the strange sense of unreality which had beset her at the time of her marriage seized on her. She noted, as they followed the Chamberlain, that the Castle was larger and more gloomy than her own home; it was quite a long way before she was asked to mount the winding staircase that led to the next storey. The Chamberlain threw open a door, and showed a small ante-room full of sunshine, which came streaming in through the lozenge-shaped lights of a broad, low casement; he then opened a door beyond, and ushered her into a large rush-strewn chamber, hung with rich tapestry, and furnished with tables and cushioned seats.

Jeanne saw two other doors, but she was too anxious for news of her husband to take much heed of her surroundings. She turned to repeat her question, but she saw only De Retz, the Chamber- lain, and Gillonne ; the Seneschal had not followed them.
"Lead me to my lord's chamber," she said to the Chamberlain. "I will seek him, as he seems to be too sick to come to me." _

There was silence. Retz sighed heavily, and looked on the ground; the Chamberlain glanced compassionately at the young Countess. "Madame," the old man said in an uncertain voice, "the Count sleeps. When her ladyship has rested after her fatiguing purney, I will again wait on her with tidings of my lord." lie bowed low; then he said a few words to Gillonne, and led her to the open doors of the other chambers; finally, with another deep reverence to his mistress, he retired, followed by Be Retz. Jeanne stood still where they had left her. Pre- sently she turned and saw that she was alone, for Gillonne had gone into the bedchamber. Jeanne followed her, but she did not glance at the room. "What docs this mean, Gillonne? My husband must indeed be ill—much worse than I was led to suppose. But why am I purposely kept away from him? Did you hear anything of this? "—for Gillonne's eyes looked full of meaning. "Is it his will, or that of others? " "I know nothing certain, dear lady • I but fear and doubt all is not well with my lord Count. Perhaps we have only to be patient. Madame is mistress here, and everyone must obey her if she asserts her authority." Jeanne bade her woman open the casements to let in fresh air. She could not keep still, but paced the room in silence. The summons to Laval had found her unwilling to quit her old home before she had performed her due period of mourn- ing; but she had told herself she should help to nurse her husband, and make acquaintance with him on his way to convalescence. "Go fetch Anne and Mathurine, my good Gillonne," she said. "The poor girls will be frighted with so many strange soldiers ; they can sleep in the other bedchamber, and you can have that cabinet beside my chamber door. The woman hesitated. "I do not care to leave madame alone in this strange house," she said.

Jeanne gave her an encouraging smile. "Come, come, Gillonne, it is not like you to teach me cowardice! This is my own home, I must therefore be safe in it. If it will make you happier, I will lock the door, when you have put the, key within the chamber." Her mistress's dignified tone made Gillonne wonder at the change that had come over her; she stood waiting outside till she heard the long key turn in the lock, then she hurried downstairs to seek for Anne and Mathurine.

"I will find out the meaning of all this before I come up again," she said. "The place looks and feels like a prison. If there is such a thing as a woman inside its walls, I shall learn all I want to know, and that quickly."

A WARD OF THE KING. By KATHARINE S. MACQUOrD, Author of "Maisie Derrick," "The Story of Lois,' "Patty," "Louisa," "At the Red Glove," "Miss Eyon of Eyoncourt," /cc.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS :—Jeanne 'Kergrist, a wealthy heiress and an only child, has become on her father's death ward of the King of France. Jeanne is only thirteen when the King commands her to marry the Count of Laval, who is twenty years her senior. The story opens in the garden of Jeanne's house, where Jeanne tells her friend and playfellow Rolland of her dislike to the proposed marriage. Rolland, a fine young fellow, disliks it too. He has been brought up with Jeanne, and, if he were richer, would marry her when she grows up. The Count of Laval comes to the castle, accompanied by a handsome young cousin, Gilles de Retz. Jeanne likes the Count, but she takes a dislike to De Retz, who flatters and pities her. He and the Count of Laval leave the castle directly after the marriage ceremony. Four years later, Jeanne's mother dies. Rolland has been away fight- ing in Italy and the Netherlands. Jeanne is alone in the world and her husband falls ill. He sends De ?Betz to fetch his young wife home to Laval.

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.
TEE JOURNEY TO LEVEL.

Gillonne stood early by her mistress's bedside. "Madame," she said, "the escort from Laval is at the gates; it has only come from Menoulas this morning, and the leader bade me say that if it is your pleasure, madame, he and his men are ready to start for Laval as soon as they have refreshed their horses. Monsieur le Comte has sent a beauti- ful litter, madame; the inner curtains are of silk broidered with golden flowers and green satin leaves; the cushions and footstools are covered with velvet from Genoa; in one corner a little mirror is set in a silver frame •, the litter is truly a dainty nest, and madame will be at her ease in it. It holds all that can be wanted on a journey. There is, besides, a waggon with stout horses to carry the chests which I have ready, filled according to my dear lady's orders before she left us."

- Jeanne gave the woman a grateful glance. "Good Gißonne," she said, "if you and my maids are ready, I will go down." .In the sorrow and responsibilities of these last months Jeanne had forgotten her childish dislike to Monsieur de Retz. Now, as he made her a reveren- tial bow when she appeared at the outer portal of Longuedec, she was pleased by his tact and good feeling in not addressing her. She looked at the litter before she entered it, and turning to Monsieur de Retz, she said she had never seen so handsome a vehicle; Jeanne loved horses, and she greatly admired the strong pair harnessed to the litter. She had already ordered that her own jennet and a horse for Gillonne should accompany the troop which was to escort her to Laval.

- -- The presence of the strange soldiers in the court- yard helped the girl through the painful leave- taking with so many old retainers, most of whom had been at the château before her birth; it was a relief to be on her way, behind the closed curtains of her litter.

The distance between Longuedec and Laval was not very much over a hundred miles, yet it took four wearisome days to reach the Château. At the first night's halt at St. Brieuc, De Retz craved permis- sion to wait on the young Countess, but Jeanne sent word that she was greatly fatigued by the long journey, and asked to be excused.

- . Gillonne took a secret pleasure in delivering this message, for De Retz had not won her good opinion; she, however, understood her mistress far too well to arouse her contradiction by a hint of her own distrust of the leader of the escort. Gillonne was a keen-witted Bretonne, she had travelled, and she was a shrewd observer. The expression of the young noble's eyes as she delivered her mistress's message disturbed her and made her inquisitive. Next morning, on the plea of leaving more room for her mistress and the two maids, Anne and Mathu- rine, in the litter, Gillonne asked leave to ride the horse provided for her. Jeanne herself would greatly have preferred riding to the slow jolting of the litter, but she was still absorbed by sorrow, and she wished to avoid conversation; she saw that by remaining in the litter she could enjoy solitude without discourtesy. Every morning, when she left her chamber to resume her place in the litter, she exch-mged a formal greeting with De Retz, and every evening, when they halted, there was her hus- band's cousin ready to hand her with the most courtly grace from her litter into the inn where they were to pass the night. Sometimes a few words passed between them, but De Retz was so quiet and sympathetic that Jeanne now looked on him as only a useful safeguard, and smiled at the fancies she had once had about him; she told her- self as she saw him from between the curtains of her litter that he was a graceful and accomplished cavalier; if she had felt less sad, she would have enjoyed a talk with him.

Giltonne rode in front of the litter, and her obser- vation made her still more uneasy; the men spoke to one another in low voices, but on the approach of De Retz their talk ceased. Many of them were, she thought, evil-looking, and these kept close to De Rd; and did not wear the expression of sullen discontent that shewed on the more honest faces of the escort.

On the third day the woman rode behind the litter to escape observation. She had determined to question a steady-looking man-at-arms, called by his comrades Gildas, and she contrived after a while to ride beside him, out of sight of the sharp-eyed leader of the troop. "This is a pleasant day," she said, "both for man and beast."

Gildas did not look at her; he muttered some- thing in a surly tone, and she left him for the time to himself. Gillonne had not always lived at Longuedeo : her parents had moved from place to place, and when, as a girl, she came to live with Jeanne's mother, she had accompanied her mistress to the Court of the good Queen Anne at Amboise, and being quick-witted, she had learnt a good deal about men and women. She was not at all dis- couraged by this first rebuff. Presently two men riding behind her began to talk. Gillonne listened, but she could not make out all they said, for they spoke in a southern patois, to winch her Breton ears were unaccustomed ; it seemed to her, however, from what she gathered that the Count de Laval's illness was more serious than she had thought it, and that they were dis- cussing the qualities of Monsieur de Retz as his successor. A little later she discovered that Gildas was hard of hearing, and could not gather the talk of the men behind. She urged her horse nearer him; she asked a few questions about their probable halting-places; bad one ? " she asked. then "Was the Count's accident a
Gildas stiffly turned his head and gazed at her up and down. The survey seemed to satisfy him: he looked pleasantly at her as he answered:

_ , ...... ..,„ ...---. "Aye, it was bad enow ; he was full of pain when we left Laval, and no wonder—the accident has cost the poor gentleman his right leg, and--" lie checked himself, and looked behind him.

Gillonne contented herself for the present with some chance remark; she pointed to a solitary mag- pie on the dreary waste they were crossing. "That sign bodes woe for some among us—a cold hearth and a desolate home." She looked keenly at her Companion.

There was doubt in his eyes as ne returned her glance, but his rugged brown face softened when he marked the earnestness of her gaze: "You have been a long while with your lady? he asked. Gillonne was accustomed to be treated with con- siderable deference by the Castle servants and the villagers of Longuedec ; the trooper's abrupt ques- tion startled her, as much as the tone of equality the man assumed towards her. "I was with my lady, but now taken to her rest, long before she gave birth to the Countess of Laval," she answered composedly. "Good!" He lowered his voice. "You are, then, ready to follow her fortunes "—he nodded towards the litter—"come what may? " "What can Come? " she answered significantly. "You said in my hearing that we shall to-morrow reach Laval ; my mistress will therefore be srfe in her husband's keeping."
_ "May the good God so will it!" He stopped and crossed himself devoutly. _ _
Monsieur de Retz had turned back from the front, and was riding towards them ; he raised his jewelled hat as he passed the litter, and then came slowly on to Gildas.
Before the leader reached them, the man said, without a glance towards his companion: "In or place:tis well tp_ keep eves and airs

div.head: CHAPTER VI. WIDOWED.
div.p: CHAPTER VI. WIDOWED.

On the morning after her arrival at Laval Gillonne told her mistress that Monsieur de Retz craved permission to speak with her. Jeanne had already sent her woman to make inquiry for the Count, but the answer was that the Count must not be disturbed. Jeanne now sent Gillonne to inquire whether the Countess could not be allowed to watch beside him; but the Seneschal, to whom the question was put, referred her to Monsieur de Retz. 'The girl hoped that this announced visit of the young noble might be the herald of better news ; at least she determined to free herself from this wearisome imprisonment, for Gillonne had advised her to keep to her own rooms, as there was so much -stir and movement in the Cast le.

While the young Countess waited for De Retz she walked round the room, and marvelled at the beauty of the tapestry. On one wall it represented the e%ploits of Achilles at the siege of Troy ; on another was depicted the visit of Ulysses to the Court of Lycornedes, and his discovery of the young but) disguised as one of the attendants of Deidttinia, Jeanne was still occupied in studying tie tigures when De Retz was shewn in. Ile bowed; then, advancing nearer, he took her hand, and touched it with his lips. " grieve to bring you very grievous tidings, infidame. Your noble husband, my honoured cousin, has passed away." Jeanne grew white under the sudden shock. She said, after a few moments: "E pray you, sir, lead me to where he lies. I will see him once more."
Dc Retz "I fear me, madame, that is no longer possible." There was horror in her eyes. She exclaimed:

"I do not •„understand you, monsieur; you have deceived me. The Count, my husband, must have been near death when you quitted Laval; why did you not warn me? Why did you hurry me away 'from Longuedec? lam mistress here, monsieur, and I demand entrance to my husband's chamber."

While she spoke, Jeanne had drawn herself to her full height. Be Retz was as much charmed by her determined spirit as lie was by her beauty, for she had become flushed with excitement. "Bo seated, madame, I pray you; grant me your patie.-)ce, for what I have to tell may at first anger You; .but iou will graciously hear ma to tine.n.d

you will, I know, acquit me Iron blame. But I ' must speak with you alone." Jeanne looked around Ler. "Where is hut Gillonne, monsieur, and she does not count;' she never leaves me." Ebe sToke brusquely,- yet with dignity; ner deter- mined look.niade De Betz aware that he must sub- ,.rnit to thto,confidant's presence. He had resolved not to 'offen4 Jeanne, and he was aware that if she chose to assert her immediate independence it would be difficult for him to influence or guide her movements, unless he resorted to force, and that would annul the hopes he cherished about her. She became impatient while he hesitated, but as she met his beseeching glance she felt ashamed to suspect him.

She seated herself; then, pointing to a chair at some distance from her own, she said gravely: "Be seated, monsieur. lam ready to hear why you declined to agree to my wish; it is but right and natural that a wife should wish to see her husband."

De Retz could hardly help smiling at the girl's ready assumption of her position ; it seemed to fit her as though she had been always mistress of Laval. Jeanne noted the grace of his movements and the sadness of his dark eyes; they were somewhat narrow, but she thought they were handsome. "Madame," he began, "in order that you may fully understand this seeming deception, I must, with your leave, speak of myself, and revert to the time when my lamented God-father first took me into his esteem." Jeanne's keen glance seemed to searc,4_his soul; but. his face remained sad and impenetriltbie. "Did he bring you up from childhood ? " she asked.

"Alas! no, madame. I wish my lot had been thus happily ordered. I believe my cousin and God-father—for he was both—had been interested, long before we met, in my welfare ; I was, however, only summoned to Laval a few weeks before I accompanied him to Longuedec." He hurried on; he did not wish her to remember the past too vividly. "On that occasion my cousin told me that he meant to provide for my future, to com- pensate for what might prove to be a disappointment to my hopes. You are perhaps aware, madame, that I now alone represent the elder branch of the house of Laval ?" The young Countess bent her head. "I intrude this on madame's notice "—he spoke more quickly—"that she may better under- stand the devoted affection and obedience I felt ',awards my lamented cousin. He was very illwhen he received the news that Madame Nergrist was near her end; and he at once sent for um. There is no time to be lost, Etienne,' he said; • a messenger must be despatched to Longuedec with a letter to announce that you are setting forth with an escort, to claim my bride and bring her to Laval. I remonstrated ; I knew that preparations for your reception had been made some time before, and that all was ready. I urged that someone might be sent in my place, or that you could be kept waiting until the Count was himself able to go to Longuedec; urged that I could not leave him while he was so suffering. He was inflexible in his determination, madame. He said he had promised your mother to claim you as soon as she had passed away, and he must keep his word. The Seneschal and the rest will care for me,' he said; and you know that our chaplain is skilful both as nurse and physician. If need should arise, I will summon the King's leech from Amboise.' I still remon- strated. I said it was a dismal time to bring a young bride home; but the Count would not listen. He said he could not bear to think of your unpro- tected position at Longuedec now that the country is known to be infested by marauders. He became at last angered by my opposition, and I had to obey, when he said that to me only could he entrust so precious a charge as the safety of the Countess of Laval."

He stopped, and looked at her. Jeanne remained ilent ; she felt unbelieving. This story sounded to her too plausible to be quite true; she felt sure that she ought to have been told the truth before she left her own home. Be Retz saw the doubt in her eyes. "Madame doubtless wonders why I did not speak of this before she quitted Longuedec • but I'had no choice in the matter; I had oniz to obey my cousin, and to escort his bride to aval. I ask you, madame, to imagine what a sore blow it was to me to learn on our arrival that the Count had passed away, and had that morning been laid in the grave of his ancestors." Jeanne's face was without expression; she felt hard and cold as a stone. "Madame will therefore—"
"Pardon me, monsieur," she said brusquely, "but I must blame you. At least I should have been told the truth on my arrival. I am not a child : this concealment was unnecessary and foolish."

She looked greatly displeased as she rose and, followed by Gillonne, turned to leave the chamber. De Retz had expected tears; perhaps petulance. The girl's stern dignity disconcerted his plans; but he recovered himself before the door closed on her. "I pray you grant me a moment, madame, and then I will no longer intrude my presence on your great sorrow." Jeanne winced; she knew that she had not shed a tear or shewn any sorrow for the death of her husband; the shock seemed to have dulled other feelings ; in the deep grief she felt for her mother this fresh bereavement did not reach her heart. De Retz went on:

"My cousin, madame, bade me remember that you are a ward of the King; his Majesty is there- fore your natural protector in your widowed state. To my sorrow, I am constrained to quit Laval on urgent business, and if you wish, madame, to seek the Ring's protection at Amboise, I will gladly escort you thither ' • if, on the contrary, you prefer to remain at Laval till you have recovered from the fatigue and the shock you have undergone, I shall feel honoured, and I need not say how welcome a guest you will be within its walls." "I thank you, monsieur, but I will go at once to Amboise ; I have a friend at Court, and I need not further burden your kindness. I thank you for your promised escort to the Court." She added this courteously ; she felt that he must have seen her anger. De Retz bowed.
"Will a horse suit you, madame, as well as a litter ; if so, we shall arrive far sooner at our destination
Jeanne smiled, and again Be Retz told himself she was beautiful.
"I should have proposed it, monsieur. lam already rested, and we can set forth whenever you summon us."

He made a low bow, and departed. When he was gone, Jeanne turned to her tirewoman: 73illonne's strong dark face looked very severe and discontented. "What ails you? " her mistress said. "What better can we do? They say we are not -tafe at Longuedec, and I certainly will not remain here, where I am evidently no longer mistress." "Your pardon, madame, but does madame forget that there is always the convent and that kind Madame de Caen, who visited my dear mistress at Longuedec when madame was still a child? While she lay ill, my dear lady told me that if you had not been married, madame, she should have pre- ferred Madame de Caen's guardianship to even that of the King." For the first time since her mother's death her old mischievous smile sparkled over Jeanne's face. "Fie, then! I am shocked at you, Gillonne! Undutifulness to the King is treason; it could not be thought of. Besides, Amboise attracts me; there I shall at last have the pleasure of embracing my long-loved cousin Francoise, Madame de Chateau- briand."

Gillonne turned sharply away, for she knew she must be looking sour; she had almost forgotten the girl's childish infatuation for the frail beauty who at that time was still the reigning favourite. The resolute Breton woman at once determined that her mistress should not be corrupted by the Court atmosphere; but she held her peace, she too well understood Jeanne's contradictory nature and her strong will ; she told herself she must get help, and there was only one person who could influence the `,Auntess of Laval. Rolland de la Touche had deserted Coetfrec ever since he had succeeded to the lordship of Orbec, close to Lisieux, and since that event he had had long spells of absence from France; she knew that the young Countess had summenenim to Longuedec when her mother lay (lying, and that the messenger brought word that the Vicomte d'Orbec was still in the Low Countries, though his return was expected. "You do not answer," Jeanne said. "What ails you, Gillonne ? " At this the woman turned and faced her mistress ; Ehe looked perplexed, but she was smiling. "I had wished to ask a favour of madame, before I knew of the sadness which has befallen at Laval. I have a cousin married at Mayenne, a place not far away, and with madame's gracious leave I could ride there and rejoin her on the way to A nlboise ; but then, if madame is to travel on horse- back, she will need me beside her? " Jeanne smiled at her.
"G-o-:--no-y good GMonne, and see your cousin, and, you peed not hasten to coon to me; I slitilin

CYCLING AND CYCLISTS.
NO. CURIOUS PHASES OF
CYCLING.
BY CHARLES E. BRANCH (ASSISTANT EDITOR. OP "TIM CYCLA.")

All the world's a cycle track, and all the people con it riders, or at least a good percentage of them are. Some are merely cyclists—members of both Sexes who use the healthful wheel solely for the pleasure they derive from it—but there are others to whom the bicycle is something more than a means to enjoyment. It is not with those cyclists who ride for pleasure that this article deals, for they are, comparatively, most uninteresting, though most sensible persons. So we will dismiss them as being nothing out of the common, and direct our attention to what may be described as the curious phases and products of cycling—rider and machine. While there exist cyclists whose sole aim in life seems to consist in riding as far and as fast as they can. there are also riders whose one object is to ride as little as possible. Truly do extremes meet in these "demon mileage riders," and these "cyclists who sever cycle," that is, in the true sense of the word. The former are common only to America, the latter Ire to be found wherever the bicycle is. The Century Club is an American institution which encourages the prostitution of a health-giving pastime by offering prizes, medals, and certificates, and last Year no fewer than seventy-two cyclists qualified for these awards. The prizes are not in themselves of great value; they are not coveted because of their antrinsic merit, but because of the "honour" that is supposed to attach to them. This will be fully appreciated when it is stated that to obtain a certificate one has TO BIDE AT LEAST 5,000 MILES IN A YEAR!

But 5,030 miles is a very small distance compared With a journey of 32,479 miles, which was the total distance ridden last year by a Mr. George, of Phila- delphia, who thus secured the gold medal offered by the club to the member covering most ground. To ride 32,479 miles in 365 days is a performance which, much as it is to be deprecated, speaks volumes for the man's physical endurance. Such a ride is equal to going nearly one and a half times round the world, and represents an average daily run of 89i miles—equal to a trip from London to Basingstoke and back. On some days, of course, this distance was not covered, while on others he Rode considerably over 100 miles per day. During the month of June, for instance, Mr. George put up 3,693 miles, an average daily spin of 123 miles. ~,,,It Was only to be expected that such a record °llld be productive of envy, that some other cyclist "n, would., be ambitious to break it, and on the first day 'Mauary a Mr. Edwards set out with this laudable zObject, and with the intention of riding 100 miles Per day to the end of the year. If he accomplishes this he will have covered 36,500 at the end of 1898, and will have added some 4,000 miles to the Previous total. Another Philadelphian rider last year covered 28,718 miles, another just 201 miles less than this, and still another 26,252 miles. The last-mentioned individual is named Irving Harrison, and he piled UP the 26,252 miles in the course of his daily work, carrying all the time upon his shoulder a ladder Weighing 251 b., which was necessary to his busi• ffess as a street lamp inspector. TURNING TO FEMALE CYCLISTS,

I May state that four women made over 5,000 miles in the year, and that the first of these covered a distance of no less than 21,026 miles. This was A. M. C. Allen. She did not ride every day in Year, but for 266 days only, so that her daily 'rage was 79 miles. This woman is the happy Se s 0 -"or of a string of "century bars" over 3ft. tlength. A "century bar" is the badge given by h -e Century Club to any member riding 100 miles right away, and Mrs. Allen, in the course of her Performance, covered 100 miles on no less than 117 occasions. This is one extreme of cycling, and from it we Will go to the other, and make the acquaintance of the cyclist who, as I have said, never cycles. This IPecies consists of young girls and old maids, who tide not because of the pleasure they derive from °Yeling, but solely for the sake of saying they do tide and shewing off their machines and costumes. these "butterflies" turn out only in sunny weather, aad are always spotlessly clean. The reader will no doubt have met them in his native town, pedalling around some fashionable aquare or crescent, or, if it be a seaside resort, COn- -6 the sea front. They never desert their local aquare or marine parade, but go round and round, or up and down, with the one object of gaining the admiration of the passers-by. But the "mileage demon" and the " butterfly " are not so numerous as those individuals who can only aPpreciate cycling when they

ARE RISKING THEIR LIVES A-WHEEL. They seem to take a fiendish delight in turning One's blood cold by their foolish feats. Ido not refer to the idiots we meet on every run, who must ride hands off through the thickest traffic, and must coast t&na every hill, though these are bad enough; but ho who are more ambitious in their desires to -u;"e11)3 Herod—who, for the sake of a little short- : notoriety, fly right in the face of death. And , ilane is legion. rrobably no man has risked his life more often in the Performance of daring feats on the bicycle than Charleser. Kilpatrick, the well-known one-legged trick rid One of his most recent flirtations with death, Will be fresh in the minds of the inhabitants of 13ouglas, Isle of Man. Just outside Douglas stands the famous Laxey Wheel, the largest water wheel io England. It is 100 ft. in height, and makes a l'evolution every forty seconds. Kilpatrick obtained Permission to have his photograph taken on the Platform at the top of the wheel, but this was not exciting enough, not sufficiently extraordinary to snit his temperament; so, holding the bicycle high above his head, he hopped on to the great water Wheel, was photographed there, and jumped back again in forty seconds. The next moment the wheel Bwong round, and had the daring cyclist been on it, ;13(1 he been one moment late, he would have been hurled to his death. ]llany people; have ridden their bicycles in the lost curious places imaginable. Some years ago a .1!r • Maltby rode his machine, one of the good Old ordinaries, along the narrow top of the Wall of the pier at Aberdeen. A slip or a deviation from the straight course and he • Would have dropped 40ft. into the sea below. L:st year a parachutist earned the distinction being the only man who ever cycled—on a safety ..,_leYCle and not on a combination bicycle flying "lachine—in the air. This was Professor Anthony, t'ho ascended by balloon at some sports at Luton. Was seated on' his bicycle beneath the silk bag gas, and attained an altitude of 4,000 ft. ere lie 11.1111 ed the cords severing the bicycle and parachute Ptla the balloon and dropped down to the earth ZFain. The feat was accomplished in safety, but "e man had a very narrow escape, owing to the °P es becoming entangled in the handlebar of the "igcle. Quite recently a Mr. Stanley C. Hart RODE A BICYCLE IN A DEN OF LIONS arid eaxne out alive, and repeated the perfomance no "3 than six times. His first expeience was at Cannes,and was the outcome of a bet between 'uroself and a friend. Tho lions' cage which he la:L! to enter was the property of the Pezon Mena- ;:t!e. and contained two of the most ferocious t7llials in Europe. They had previously killed 47e men, including the original proprietor of the b.enagerie. The cyclist entered the cage on one ItYcle wheeling another, which he kept between ilizos e f and the lions, whilst riding in a semi- circle the front part of the cage. Of course the o'railemer accompanied him out, but this:did not prevent Wheel the lions wiping the spokes of the front Of one of the bicycles with his paw. tuci is Possible to go on relating such feats to the ke of the article, but I will conclude with the sohrit,ti°ll of a Mexican toreador who attempted to hnll on a bicycle in the arena in the city of

But he was not the first of his kind to attempt this sort of thing, for as far Lack as itS69 velocipedes were tried in the arena, at Nimes, without, however, much success. Numerous and queer are the uses to which the bicycle has been put by ingenious individlials from time to time. By the attachment of a sail the bicycle can be converted into a veritable land ship, and cycle sailing, as an exhilarating and exciting pastime, wants a lot of beating. Its only rival is ice-cycling, for which specially designed machines are built in America. Most people are aware that

div.head: HUNTING ON A BICYCLE
div.p: HUNTING ON A BICYCLE

has been indulged in, and they have, no doubt, heard how Mr. O'Brien, M.P., who was following a fox hunt on a bicycle in County Meath, was, by great good luck, the first in at the death. This gentleman may have been said to have set the fashion in following the hunt on a bicycle. The tricycle has also been used for sporting purposes, a gentleman having adapted it to bird shooting. His modus operandi was to cover the front of his machine With bushes, behind which, seated on the saddle, he was hidden from the gaze of the birds whose suspicions were not aroused as he drew near by what appeared to be only a moving bush. By this means he was able to get within closer range than he otherwise could have done.
One reason of the bicycle's world-wide popu- larity is that it can be so adapted that
ANTON& CAN RIDE IT.

from the youngest to the eldest, from the smallest to the largest; and even the blind and the crippled are not debarred from its en- joyment. It will come, no doubt, as a revela- tion to many that there are blind cyclists, and that there are several devoid of sight who: ride their machines without any extraneous aid. The Suffolk town of Beccles boasts perhaps the most perfect blind cyclist in the world, a young man named Tracy, who had the terrible misfortune to lose his sight at the age of four. When he goes out for a spin someone always accompanies him, but he steers his machine himself, and is enabled by his keen sense of hearing to pick his way alone. Most of the inmates of the Royal Normal College and Academy of Music for the Blind, at Norwood; are cyclists, and go out in parties, sometimes riding as far as Brighton, Derby, and Birmingham. These cyclists, however, do not ride by themselves, but With sight to steer them. six, eight, ten, and taNrvee lsve ea t ewdi t ohn a mmaaenh ibnleess sed holdingwt Of cycling cripples—armless, legless, one-armed, one-legged—there is no end; they are, in fact, as numerous as the "youngest cyclist in the world " or "the smallest cyclist in the world," which every country has in its turn produced. The distinction of being the smallest cyclist belongs without doubt to a tiny Cuban girl, who is just 26in. in height. Count Magri, of Rome, is another midget wheelman; he stands 30in. high. On the: other hand there are Messrs. Grimes and Bliss, who were in this country recently acting as living advertisements for certain makes of American machines; taken all round they are probably the biggest men who have ever ridden bicycles. Bliss stands 61t. siin. in height, and turns the scale at over 30st. While Grimes is 61t. sin. tall, and weighs 36st. As curious as some of the incidents;and individuals referred to above are some of the machines that have been constructed, mostly for purposes', of advertisement. Magnitude has been aimed at in some instances, lavish display in others. The biggest tricycle in the world was built by an American Tyre Company, and weighed I,Boolb. The side wheels stood 141 t. high and the front wheel 71 t., and were fitted with tyres, having a diameter of 15in., and Bin. respectively. Eight men were required to move this mass. The world's largest bicycle was produced by a Yankee cycle firm, and stood over 20ft. in height. The saddle alone was large enough to accommodate a full-sized bicycle. Last, but by no means least, there is the costliest bicycle ever built. The sum of L 2,000 was spent upon it, and the firm commissioned to manufacture it turned out a very handsome and elaborate machine. All joints and connections were covered with gold, artistically inlaid with precious stones. The name plate was a blaze of diamonds, and on various parts of the tubing embossed on gold, and embellished with diamonds, pearls, and rubies, were depicted all descriptions of racing. WELSH COAL CRISIS.

div.head: HOW THE MEN BUFFER.
div.p: HOW THE MEN BUFFER.

THE strike among the Welsh coal miners has recently assumed so serious a character that an incalculable amount of suffering has been borne by these workers, and the notice of the whole nation has been dtawn to the conditions of their work. But even at the best of times miners have much to bear. As an instance, there is a young man named James Thomas, twenty-six years of age, living at 6, Baxter-terrace, Glyncorrwg, South Wales. When ques- tioned by a" Bridgend Chronicle" reporter, he stated : " Whilst busy at work underground, about ten years ago, I was seized with violent pains in the back, and after that was subject to terrible spells of pain at inter- vals. I was incapacitated from work for a fortnight at a time, but about eighteen months ago I became so bad that I had to give up work altogether. I consulted a doctcr, and attended Cardiff Infirmary, where I was told my complaint was the collier's bane—lumbago. For many hours we have to labour cramped up, with water dripping from the roof, and at all times on damp earth. At that time I could neither sit, stand, nor lie down without suffericg herrible pain, and when my mother accompanied me to the Infirmary she thought I would die in the train. One day my father came across an advertisement of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and we then decided to try them." " With what result 2" queried the pressman. " After the filet box of the Pills I found some relief, which encouraged me to try a second ens, when there was a marked improvement ; my limbs became easier, my appetite returned, and soon, after taking six or seven boxes, I felt healthier than I had done for many months. I. feel convinced that if I hadn't taken Dr. Williams' Pink Pills I should never he where lam now. I am stronger and healthier than over I was." THIS AFFAIRS OF A VV.IIOLESALR CLOTHIER, At the Manchester County Court on Monday be- fore His Honour Judge Parry, Mr. J. H. Hutt, clothier, appeared to answer a judgment summons issued by Messrs. J. S. and J. Greenhalgh, ot Roch- dale, for the sum of .£l2 15s. The debtor stated that he had assigned the whole of his estate, valued at £22,000, for the benefit of his craditots. Having thus given up all he possessed, he thought the plaintiffs ought to share with the other creditors. —Mr. Marsh (Messrs. Crowther and Marsh), who appeared for the judgment creditors, said Mr. Hutt obtained goods from his clients two or three days before the assignment was made. He understood that Mr. Hutt was employed at a good salary by a committee of his creditors. Mr. Hutt said it was not yet settled what his salary was to be. He was manager to a company to whom the trustees had sold his former business So far he had received a salary of .£3 a week.—Mr. Hutt admitted also that Mrs. Hutt was carrying ow a small business,but she was liable for £4OO as security under the assign- ment, and her estate was only worth £2oo.—The Judge said he was satisfied that an assignment had been made for the benefit of the creditors. He should only make a small order.—f or XI a month.

div.head: THE
div.p: THE
ASSAULT BY A WARRINGTON CAB PROPRIETOR.
ALL ABOU I' A LANDAU

At ...he Warrington Borough Curt on Fridey morning bernre the Mayor (Alderman Wright) and other magis- trates, a croeresumrnone was heard in which P %trick Meginn, cab propristor, of Sankey-street. was charged with assaulting William Timmins, of 5, E iqaceee rest, on July Ist, and Timmins was charged with asks-saltine Maginn at the same time and place.--Mr. A. Browne represented Timmins, and Mr. Forehaw appeared for Maginn. Ii opening the case Mr. Browne sal Mr. William Tirnmint was cashier to Mr Pendlebury and he mai his father-in law—a very respectable man named Mather— desired to go to Barnhill on Walking Day. Mr. Timeline was accustomed to driving and die not wish t.be accompanied by a driver. Be engaged a landau tor 101 Be, and paid the money and got a receipt for it, the landau to be in use from twelve none until the return to Warrington. Mr. Timmins sent his brother-in-law for the landau. Maginn said it was ready, but wanted him to have a driver. He refused, and deteridanc gave the money Back. It was taken to the complainant, and he and his father-in-law went to see Mr. Maginn, who told cempleinant he ceold not have the vehicle with- out a licensed driver. His (Me. Browne's) client replied that was all nonsense, and that he was not compelled to have a licensed driver. Defeudant said something very foolish, that he knew mere than the cemplainaut did, and snatched the bill out of the old man's hand. Complainant got hold ef the defendant's wrist and got the receipt back again, remarking to the defendant that he was nothing but a scamp to take a bill out of a mm's hand like that. Defendant said to Timeline, " Well, if you were not on decent ground I would give you two black eyes." Ti this complainant replied,"Welecome on indecent ground and see what you can dc ." Mr. Maginn went up the yard and his client foolishly followed, when the defendant picked up a pikel and struck him on the head with it, rendering him unconscious. When he recovered he went to the Police Station, and the Chief Constable kindly dressed his wound. He was subeeepiently atten ded by Br. Geary. What defence there could be to this assault he did not know. There Spointing to the compla:eiant) is the man with the heal—the broken head. (Laughter). He has been ill far three days acid hardly able to attend to his work. The complainant gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement.—ln answer to Mr. Fershaw, com- plainant admitted that he called the defendant a scamp, but he did not hit him at all. He did not deserve the punishment he received. Thomas Mather, 70, New-road, father-in-law to the complainant also gave evidence. He said there was no landau in the place when they got there. There was only a large 'bus. William Ormson, 5, Qeay-fold, and John Clare also gave evidence on behalf on the complainant. The Chief Constable having been sworn, said he ex- amined the complainant's wound, which was abrut an inch and a quarter long. It was deep, jagged and long, and the blow must have been a severe one. The man had lost a great quantity of blood. Mr. Forshaw, for the defence, said he admitted an assault was committed, but contended that there was great provocation. It was Timmins who was the aggressor. He was frequently told to go off the pre- mises, but he would not do so and used abusive languaee. He was tcld that no landau would be sent out without a driver. He called Mr. Maginn a dishonest man, a scoundrel, and a scamp, and to get out of the way of the man his client walked away, but Timmins followed him, and Was about to strike Magian when the latter, in self-defence, did strike Timmins. Mr.Maginn said he wishes to give a plain unvarnished etaterrient of what took place. In the course of a long statement he said he had no money dealings with Tim mine and his father-in-law. When they cams upon the scene it was an hour and 20 minutes after the landau bad been refused to a person whom they sent. They did not want to have a driver, and witness told them the landau could not be sent out without Ore. They called him bad names, and he walked away from them and came back again. They hustled hint round the office. The most decent thing they said about him was that he , was a scoundrel. He received great provocation, and believing he was about to be assaulted he admitted that he struck Timmins. The complainant then said " Now I have you ; you will pay dearly for this." Harry Whitney, employed by Mr. Maginn, and John Lae gave evidence of on assault having been committed upen Mr. Maginn when he was in the office by Timmins and his father-in-law. The Bench retired from the court to censider their decitien. On their return, The Mayor said : We have carefully considered this matter, and we are satisfied that an assault has been committed, and that it has been rather a SCIIOII3 one. But I think we are all of the opinion that you (Mr. Maginn) have received great provocation. Therefore the decision is that you be fined 20s. and costs. The magistrates allowed an advocate's fee of 10e fid. Mr. Forshaw : What about the assault on Mr. Magian ? Evidence has been given that he was assaulted.
The Mayor Timmins will be fined in the costs, 103 Bd. Timmins when paying the fine remarked that it was a "downright shame." He never put a hand on Magion,

div.head: ROWE.
div.p: ROWE.
PRINCE OF WALES DISTRIBUTES AWARDS OF THE ORDER OF ST. JOHN.

On Friday last week the Prince of Wales, Grand Prior of the Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem in England,preSented,ln the salmon at Marlborough House, medals and certificates of honour to those who had dur- ing the past year saved life on land at imminent personal risk. In each case the Earl of Lathom, G.C.B. (Chan- cellor of the Order),announced the name of the recipient. A short statement of the act of bravery was read by Captain Sir Alfred Jenhson, R.N. (Secretary-General of the Order), and Mr. R. H. Mac Lean (Genealogist of the Order) handed the medal and certificate en a cushion to his Royal Highness. Henry Rowe (Warrington) was presented with a bronze medal for very courageous r;onduct displayed on July 24, 1897, in stopping a runaway horse, attached to a driverless cab, as it was on the point of dashing into a precession of children, blocked in a thoroughfare,known as Sankey-street, Warrington. Rowe pulled the horse down and fell beneath it, sustaining severe internal in- juries. Had it not been for Rowe's prompt and heroic action the horse would hays plunged right into that part of the procession then parading Sankey-street, and loss of life must have ensued, owing to the crowded state of the thoroughfare.

The trale circles of ths cycling vrorld are much excited by the nerve of another great s'ru.zgle im- pending betwein tyre comoanies. Tne Palmer Tyre has blen ma le under a licen.e from the Dunlop Company, since the latter bought up the Clincher patents. This liceuQe has within the last few days oiseit revoked, the Dunlop Company asserting that the Palmer Company has sublet the rizlate contrary to the terms of the license,and sold the Lyrae at a lower figure than that mutually agreed upon. The Palmer people absolutely deny both allegationv,and farther quote a decision in the courts some little time back by Mr. Justice Stirling,under which they can sell as cheaply as they like. In the meantime they will ignore the action of the Dunlop firm until the case comes up in court,as it will do very shortly. As both firms aro rich,or, at any rate, can command plenty of capital,the light bids fair to be both long and desperate It is doubtful, however, whether the lawyers will not derive m)re profit from it than either of the diEputantk

Dr. Llorton, one of the most distinguished and highly re4pecter: Nonconformist divines in the n.etropo!is, has struck out a new departure—in this part of the world at least. He had arranged a convention at Hampstead of a number of Noncon- formist village ministers, for deliberation on all the matters conn..cted with their pastoral work in their respective vi:lages. Nearly the whole of the week just ended has been devoted to conferences on the subject, and a great deal of interesting matter of a theological, pastoral, and social character, as to the villa gore and Nonconformist work among them, has been accumulated. There were about 30 country ministers and evangelists present in town,who were all lolged and boarded by members of Dr. Horton's congregation free of expense, while their account of their experience has been invaluable to Dr. Horton and the other London ministers who met thein conference. They must have urn back to their villages with minds enlarged and stimulate 1.

Nelson', practice when disagreeable signals were hoisted of chipping the telescope to his blind eye is faithfully imitated by members of the Government. Not long taco Lord Salisbury set the example by pleadine that he had not read gr. Chamberlain's notorious speech at Birmingham. A few days later Mr. Chamberlain declined to discuse Lord Saliebury's speech, on the .ground that he had I omitted to supply himself with a copy of the de- liverance. On Monday Mr. Balfour, following the ' lead of his cellsegues, brought an unseeing eye to bear on the extremely inconvenient report of the Old Age Pensions Committee. The document, he urged,h as just been issuecyind the Government had not had time to reflect on its very important conei- derations. ,6 In any case,' he jauntily added, "the matter could not be dealt with in the course of the present session." A ripple of ironical laughter passed along the Opposition benches Mr. Chamber. lain looked as if he should like to resent the demon- stration. l was aimed at him, and he knew it.

The sudden resignation of Lord Arthur Hill has given rise to more gossip in the lobby than it is possible to describe. It is regretted greatly by the general body of Unionists, by whom, as a Whip as well as personally, he was greatly esteemed. His urbanity and courtesy in the discharge of trouble- some duties are acknowledged by all Nlinisterialists, who are puzzled beyond measure to account for his unexpected retirement from Parliament. So far as the public know, this has come about within 24 hours. That there is some cause which is not con- venient to make known vvidely believed, and a cause of this kind can only be dissatisfaction on his part with the Irish policy of the Government. That is the explanation which one everywhere :meets with as to the sudden step he has taken. It is I ridiculed in the closer Ministerial circles, where it is asserted that his resignation has been for a con- sidereble time in prospect. If so. the secret has been well kept. What his dissatisfaction with the policy of the Coreenment can be is a source of mystery to everybody. If it is founded on the Local Government Bill, he is rather late in making up his mind to resign. His resignation also in- volves the loss of a substantial salary as Comptroller of the Household. All the probabilities are against any defection from the Government in a fit of petulance or of temper. Tha leaders of the party would not allow a man who had solved so long and so well to retire without some recognition of his valuable work.

Several members of the Cabinet are secretly de- lighted at the breakdown of the old-age pensions scheme. If the committee had been able to bit up- on a plan with some feasibility in it, it would have led to an attempt at legislation next Session, unless it had broken down under public criticism during the recess. It is certain enough that ' the decision of the committee has removed a grievous load from the mind of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The policy was accepted by the Conservative party at , the last general election, less from conviction than a pious desire to be the champion of a social pro- gramme adopted out of deference to Mr. Chamber- lain, and as a kind of seal and symbol of the union of the two wings of the party. By the appoint- ment of the committee and by the committee's failure, after a prolonged inquiry, to find a reason- able scheme, the conscience of the Tory members is now discharged from its obligations. and one already sees that any attempt at legislation would disclose disunion. The Tory wing will not follow further this Liberal lJnionist policy, and Mr. Cham- berlain's influence with his alliea is not quite what it was when he was supposed to be taking tricks in his controversy with President Kruger.

Touching the new Vaccination Bill and the supPY of glycerinated vaccine lymph, I bear that arrangements have been made whereby the lymph will be supplied to I.ie practitioner in a glass tube contained in a covering tube of white metal, which latter will be sealed with a gummed label bearing the name of the individual to be vaccinated the date of sealing, and the mark of the Government depart- ment. This seal will be a guidance to the parent or guardian of the child of the purity of the lymph. As to the prospects of the billot is not unreasonable to suppose that the Government, rather than sacri- fice the measure,will give way to the demand for the insertion of Sir Walter Foster's provision for ex- emption en declaration of conscientious objection. An amendment to Sir Walter's clause, to be moved by Colonel Long, would be accepted by the anti- vaccination party as a compromise. The proposal is to make relief difil. cult for the person who has a conscientious objection by rsquiriog him or her to go before two magistrates sitting in petty sessions for it. It is held that this provision would inflict no hardship, inasmuch as any person whose objec- tion is really a conscientious and not a frivolous one would not object to take the trouble to give effect to it. lf• the Government accept this con- science clause in its amended form the opponents of the bill would probably drop all other objections and the bill would be safe.

The movement inaugurated by Mr. Chamberlain for exhibiting the samples of foreign-made articles which were competing with British-made goods in colonial markets, and beating us in territory which was pre-eminently our own, is now peeping into the hands of the Board of Rrade, or, to be more pre- cise of its Commercial Intelligence Committee of whose labours, as yet, the country has not seen any repuits. The exhibitions at the London Chambers of Commerce are closed, and the peripatetic exhibi- tions are slso at an end. Those samples which were sent into the provinces have come back to town, and will probably form part of a permanent museum, and be supplemen,ed from time to time by fresh samples obtained from the colonies. The idea, I believe,is to make the museum applicable to the compatitien we have to encounter in all quar- ters of the globe, and to form an object lesson illus- trative of the enterprise of our rivals and of our own defects.

The Lord Mayor has issued invitations to all the members of the Press Gallery of the House of Com- mons to dinner at the Mansion House on the 30th instant. This is one of the highest compliments yet paid to members of the Gallery, who number con- siderably over 200,and is an indication of the status which the Gallery has, for a considerable number of years past, been taking in the profession of journal- ism. At the Gallery dinner, which took place at Brighton a few weeks ago, the Lord Mayor was a guest, and enjoyed himself in the heartiest manner. lie was probably struck with the fact that the members are not Bohemians in the sense of setting social usages at defiance,like so many men attached to literature, music, and painting ; aid the present invitation has grown out of his experience on that occasion.
