div.p: LYME WESLEYA.N CHURCH.
GRAND FLORAL BAZAAR.

Sir William Cutsliffe Brooks-,-Ifir-t.., and Lady Brooks opened a grand floral bazaar in the Drill Hall, Lymto, on Tnursday last week. The bazaar had been promoted by the Vi'esleyans of Lymm, with a three-fold object in view, namely, to provide unds to purchase a new organ for the Lymcn Wes- leyan Church ; to make necessary alterations to receive the same; and to cover other needful im, provements in the frust property. The Drill Hall lends itself admirably tor the purposes of a bazaar, and on this occasion the interior was made particu- larly attractive. The decorations had been carried out entirely by Mrs. and Miss Chorley, of Heatley. Art muslins of various colours had been used in the decoration of the stalls, and by the introduction of curtains and screens, cosy corners had been provi- ded where the visitors could partake of refresh- ments and enjoy a tete•a-tete conversation. On the platform plants and fl)wera had been brought into use in the representation of a woodland scene which was much aimired. The whole ensemble was pleasing to the eye, and reflected credit on all concerned. A. vane I assortment of goods—usually seenat bazaars—decked the stalls which were at- tended to by ladies conn.cted with the church and school. Excellent arrangements had been made for the bazaar by strong committees and the following officers :—Chairman, Mr E Brown, sent ; treasurer, Mr James Dodds; secretary, Mr H S Brown. The Stewards were Messrs Wm Clarke, Jas Clarke, Thos Jones, S Heathcote, jPicton, F 0 Roston, John Winstanley, P Warburton, John Wilkinson, John Wilkinson junr. . . _
The stalls and stallholders were as follows :

Congregational stall (No. I) in charge of Mrs. Dodds, assisted by Mrs. Clarke. Miss C arks, Miss Dodds, Mrs. Elliott, Mrs. Heathcote, the Misses Heathcote, Mrs, Jones, Mrs. F. 0. Moston, Mrs. Pickton, Mrs. Reid, and Mrs. Peter Warburton.
Congregational stall (Ni. H) superintended by Mrs. Brown assisted by Mrs. E. Brown, junior, Mrs. Ferris, M 195 fiolfurd, Mrs. Meldrum, Mrs. Surtees, and,Mrs. Whitfield.

Choir and Scholars stall: Miss Rawlinsen assisted by Mies Brookes, Miss Jones, Miss Padgleam, the Misses Winstanley, with choir members and senior scholars. Flower and Plant stail: Miss Daisy Warburton, assisted by Miss Chorley.Miss Ethel Mosta°, Miss Carrie Pickton, and Miss Louie Warburton. Refreshment Stall and Tea Room :—Refreshment : Mrs. Winstanley assisted by Miss Brown, Mrs. Burrows, Mrs. H. S. Brown, Mrs. Chorlev, Mrs. Lord, Miss Reid, and Miss M. Warburton. Tea Rocan : The mem Machin, assisted by Mrs. E. Eazlehurat, Mrs. Isaac Maires, Miss Mareland, Mrs. Perrin, Mrs. RogersomMies Redrnayne, and Miss Whitfield. Shortly after two o'clock on Thursday afternoon Sir William Brooks, Bart, and Lady Brooks performed the opening ceremony. Amongst those present were :—The Rev. J. Gunnell (Penketh), Mrs. Norris, Mrs. James Dodds' Mr. and Alre. Edwin Brown,Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Richardson, Mr Johnson Lightfoot, Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Brows, jun, Mr. H. J. Brown, Mr. W. H. Finch, Mr. W. H. Finch, jun. Mrs. T. Chorley, Mrs. Z. Crosfield, Mr. E. Weston, Mr. F. 0. Moston, Mr. and Mrs. Surtees, Mrs. William Pearson, Mr. and Miss Masters, Mrs. Pick. ton, Mrs. W. C. Nicholson, Mrs Harbottle,Mrs. Holferd, Miss Shaw Green, Miss Winifred Hayward, Mrs. Percy Sticock, Mrs. Rymer Young, Mr. Arthur Finch and others. The proceedings commenced with the singing of a hymn, after which the Rev John Gunnell introduced Sir William and Lady Brooks to the meeting. In doing 60 he said it had been his pleas re as well as his duty to take part in a goodly number of opening ceremonies at bazaars, and he had always noticed that those who took part in them did well te curtail their remarks. Happily the duty devolving upon him did not require many words to give force to it. The honour had been alloted him by the committee of introducing to them Sir William and Lady Brooks. They scarcely needed any introduction. Both Sir William and Lady Brooks had served them admirably in the past, and most of those present would have a grateful recollection of tha prominent part taken by them in a similar func- tion eight years ago. (Hear, hear.) It was a very courteous and kindly thing of Sir William and Lady Brooke to come and repeat their kindness to the Wesle- yens of Lymm who were trying to do a little good in the parish and surrounding neighbourhood. He would now introduce Sir William and Lady Brooks, and place the further guidance of the ceremony with Sir William. (Applause.) Sir William Brooks, who was cordially received, said it gave himself and his wife very great pleasure to come amongst them again. He remembered—and happily his memory was very retentive—the time when they so kindly welcomed him eight years ago,and when became to do his dety in assisting them at the commencement of the work which had now been carried out. Though it had been carried out so well still there was always something wanting. That was in the nature of things, and they were not exempt from the common law. They had found that their organ was not worthy of them nor worthy of the great object for which it had been dedicated. And it had been deter:nined—and very wisely determinrd—that they should have a better organ and a better place in which to receive it, so that they might with that well-known fondneas for devoting the voice of praise to God, carry on the worship of God more decently and in order. It was for this purpose that the bazaar had been organised. For tunately the organisers had been able to secure the assistance of ladies without whom no good thing, no great thing ever was done. (Hear, hear, and applause). It would give Lady Brooks and himself very great pleasure to go round the stalls and observe what had been done, and also give assistance to the work they bad in view, by purchasing some of the nice things they saw had been made by clever heads and nimble fingers, acid willing hearts. (Applause). He hoped their gathering there that day would have the result of providing sufficient money to carry out the good work for which the bazaar was intended. (Applause). After prayer had been effered, Miss Adelaide Mary Dodds stepped forward to present Lady Brooks with a handsome bouquet. Mr. Edwin Brown proposed a vote of thanks to Sir William and Lady Brooks for their presence, referring to the great assistance they gave them at the Wesleyan bazaar eight years ago. Mr. Moston seconded the vote of thanks which was passed with hearty approval. Sir William Brooks having fittingly acknowledged the compliment, the sale then commenced. Numerous attractions were provided. Mies Gertrude Shaw Green held consultations in palmistry in a species tent. Another feature was what was termed a " guess cake." The competitors were entitled to lift the cak end judge of its weight. The person who guessed the correct weight was to take the cake. A smoke room was arranged to the right of the platform for the benefit of those who enjoy a whiff of the favourite weed. The entertainments included the cinematograph or animated Pictures which were exhibited in the lecture hall, speci- ally prepared for the purpose. There was also an American "Freak " side show "in conjunction with the time-honoured art gallery," A shooting saloon with guns, slugs, and targets provided, had been erected. Short concerts were given each evening and freely pat- ronised. Mention should also be made of the ladies sun- light washing competition, and the gentleman's hat trimming campetition which caused roars of laughter. Oa Friday,the bazaar was again opened. The proceed- ings were presided over by Miss Bessie Mitten, and Mrs. G. Lyttleton Dewhurst, opened the bazaar. STOCKTON HEATH.

WALKING DAr.—This event is an auspicious one to the children, and is looked forward to for some con- siderable time. Happily in Stockton Heath their anxiety was set at rest early on Friday by the appearance of a cloudless sky, which fulfilled its prognostications during the day.A short service was held at St. Thomas's Church at a quarter to two e'clock. The procession consisting of scholars of St. Thomas' Sunday and Day school and the Non-conformist chapels to the number of about 800 headed by the Wilderspool baad, proceeded up Elles- mere-road, Lawrenson's Brow,down Whitefield-roacband then through the village. Tea was arranged for the infants in the Church Room. There was a very con- siderable increase in the number of children above last year, which fact must be very gratifying to thes teachers of the school. The older children were provided with tea later. Alter tea the whole of the scholars proceeded to a field kindly lent by the Wilderspool Brewery, where games, etc., were indulged in till 9 o'clock, when the bell rang and the Doxology was sung. A very pleasant day was brought to a close, thanks to the willing help always forthcoming on such occasions.

A young man. named William Woods, was on Saturday night found dead in his house in Greyrock-street, Liverpool, having been burned through. it is supposed, a suspended lighted oil lamp in the kitchen falling upon him and setting his olothes on fire.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON
TRAINING COLLEGE.

ANNUAL PRIZ it DISTRIBUTION. The annual eveet of the distribution of prizes to the students of the Warrington Training (klege took place on S eturday afterneon. The Rev, T. W. Sharpe, OW, late Senior Chief Inspector, took the chair. There were also present on the platform, the very Rev the Than of Manchester (hon. secretary to the Training College), the Rev Morley Stevenson (Principal of the College), the Rev Canon Penrhvn, the Rev. Canon Willis, Dr. Watkias (Newton-le-Willows), Mr S E Haworth, and Mr Efance (clerk to the Liverpool School Board). Toe following also accepted invitations ;—The R9V and Han C F Cross, the Re. Charles E Jackson (Rector of Nantsrich), the Rev E J Willcocks, the Rev H V and Mrs Pigot, the Roy H R and Mrs. llartwrielt, the Rev F • Screeton, the Rev EC E and Mrs Carleton, the Rev S P and Mrs Gray, the Rev J and Mrs Bell-Cox (Liverpool), the Rev if and Mns Brierley, the Rev A A Markham, the Rev W E Blythe, Mr. D anbc(ederic to the Widnes School Board), Mrs Be stnont,Mrs Steivenson,Mrs Penrhyndiirs Willio,Miss LAX (Ormskirk), Mrs Hunter (Ormskirk), Miss Massy, Mils Combe, Captain, Mrs and Mies Withingten, Mr, Mn, and Miss Woods (Walton), Mr C White, the Misses Whit" Mrs and Kiss Colton, Miss M Timswell, Dr and Mrs Guest Goruall, Dr and Mrs Sherratt, Mrs and the MiS36.l Broadbent, Mr and Mrs J D Buckton, Mns Sharp, Mrs Hodgson, Dr and Mrs Adams, Mrs and the Misses Litton, Mn, Mrs and Miss May, Mr Raddock, the Misses Watkins,Mr and Mrs Carruthers,Mr and Mrs R Johnson, Miss Kennedy, Mrs Flood, Mrs Harry, Miss Kenyon, Mr and Mrs W S Woods, Miss Lester,Miss Smith, Mr Turner korrinisieg inspector for the Liverpool Diocese), and about two hundred parents and friends of the students. The college staff was represented by the fellosving ; the Rev. H. A. Lester (lecturer), Miss Ferrimen (lady su- perintendent of the Hostel), and the Governesses (Miss Timewell, Miss Perry, Miss Bell, Miss Brooks, and Miss Broadbent). _ _

The PUNCITAL, in introducieg the Chairman (the Rev. T. W. Sharpe) said he had not only been an inspector but an inspector of inFpectors, a chief inspector. He had been for many years an inspector of training col- leges, and though not of training colleges fer girls, he knew what a training college ought to be and could speak to them as they should be spoken to on the subject. In the name of himself aad the cotninittee he expressed the pleasure it gave him to see so many vieitors present. Oa those occasions they always welcomed the parents and relatives and friends of their students. They liked them to see something of the inside of the building in which their daughters were trainee. He did not know whether there was anything very special to record in the history of the college during the past year, except it was the resignation of Miss Goddard, who had been linked with the intereate of the college for a period of forty years Previously as governess and latterly as lady superintendent, ebs had devoted herself levelly to the interests of those under her care in both capacities. He had lost during the last year his colleague Mr. Rater, who was now principal of the Training College of Derby. During the four years Mr. !deter had been with them, he bad rendered them most efficient help. Though they were glad of his pro- motion, they regretted his leaving. Such partings from the various members of the staff must occur, but they could not help regretting the severance of those,whe had worked with them in lone and loyally. He took that opportunity to express their regret at the loss of these who bad left and also t s publicly acknowledge how deeply they were indebted to all the members of their staff. (Applause.) With the Principal of a college 'everything depended on his staff. They could be the Igreatest possible help and they might be anything bat a help. He had said before, and he now repeated that he did not think any principal had been se blessed with a helpful and loyal staff during the the whole time of his offiee.as he had been,and he tendered his thanke to them en that public occasion. (Applause.) The statistics of ' this examination, showed that in their religious know- ledge examination of that year, they had established what was,he believed, in the parlance of the day,a re- cord. (Hear, hear.) They had done what they had never done before. The great majority of their students had been placed in the first Clais, only a few in the se- cond, and none at all in the third. (Applause.) He would also add that their other examinations had been most satisfactory. The principal of a college was sup- posed to be an old fogey, and was not supposed to be aware that there were such thins as games—(laughter) —but during the last year they had had an outburst of games which he thought was due to the inspiration of the old fogey. (Applause.) He did like to see young people playing games whatever old fogies might think. In his opinion they had not done enough in past years for their tele sol children in the matter of games. They had turned them out into playgrounds and let them look after themselves. He hoped that the students would go out of that college able to teach and also to teach games so that the children would be intellectually and physi- cally more capable of performing their duties in after life. (Applause.) They would be surprised to know the number of games the students indulged in at the col- lege. He could asswee them, and he was pleased to be able te say it, thit judicious recteation formed no small part of the education of their students. (Applause.) The Rev, T. W. Snub% who was received in a very cordial manner, said he was reminded last week that once upon a time he was an inspector of training col- leges,and was astonished to end that ix the year 1876 he had advised a young man not to matriculate at the university. His advice Co youee people now was to matriculate if they possibly could. Matri- culation was now within the reach of any young man or woman who had been fairly taught before their admission to the College. He would be glad to see all examinations when out of the hands of the Elucation Department and placed in the hands of the Universities. He would welcome such a change as that beceuse it would secure a liberal educa- tion both before and after. It was written in the record of the Educational Department that a building merely rectatagular in shape was at one time quite sufficient for the education of the working classes. They were ignor- ant of the laws of ventilation, and people of the present doy had something to learn in that respect. WWI one came to think of it there was no each thing as a play- ground in the whole of England attached to a school. He was the author of that clause in the Lot which Gott - pelted the manag,ars of every school to give ten minutes' play to the children each morning and afternoon. Schoolrooms had been Wonderfully improved since the early days, and now compared favourably with those en the Continent. The Prussian elementary code allowed sir cubic feet of air space for each child, whereas they in England allowed ten. The Prussians put three big boys into the space allowed by them to three is 'bias. In their modern teaching they came much in contact with Dame Nature, and the more they came into contact with nature the more true would be their teaching. Speaking of the great importance of natural science, Mr. Sharpe Said it introduced young people to realities, and made them think of what they saw around thorn. It taught them to observe and to reason from what they saw. Another fault was the excessive amount of chattering , which went on in the schools. It was called by the euphonius name of oral teaching. (Laughter.) Oral teaching was limited in one reepect because he found that three oral lessons were as much as any human throat could give utterance to in the Course of a day. That kind of teaching had grown so much that he was bound to say the children leaving their elementary sehoole were so little taught in the art of acquiring knowledge that they did not pass in large numbers to the continuation schools. They had lost all power ef thinking for themselvea. No knowledge was worth anything unless it had bees acquired by mental effort of their own. For all the changes that had taken place though there was room for improvement yet, they had not arrived at anything like finality, and though the young women there had to be thankful for fifty years of progress, they would have much to struggle against. He should like to see a free passage from the primary to the secondary schools for all scholars. The classes in some schools were far too large for the teachers to have a chance of studying individual character. How thank- ful they felt for the religious life of these colleges. They wanted religions teaching by religious persons and the associations the student formed there, were associations that influenced their whole life. (Applause). div.head: MESSRS, PETER WALKER AND SON'S EXCU FtSION
div.p: MESSRS, PETER WALKER AND SON'S EXCU FtSION

One of the pleasantest and bt menseied excur- sions promoted by any fi-itt in Warrington was that provided for the enanlova I at the Warrington breweries of Meesrs. Peter Walker and Son.who had their annual trip" to 'th watter--iide " oa Saturday. A better day for the occasion there could not have been. Bright sunshine and a slight breezes con- duced to make the conditions SR favourable as any- one could wish. The programme fo- this year was also excellent in every respect. First to Southport by train, a stay of four hours here, and then on to Blaekpool by boat, and the same pro- cedure in returning provided a treat in which variety ' and change were prominent features. The employ6s from I the King-street and Dallan-lane Breweries numbered about 800 and were accompanied by the manager (Mr. ' J. Fulton Smith), Mr. John Baird (head brewer, Dallam- lane), Mr. John Dunn (bead brewer, King-street), Mr. Arthur Potter (cashier) and the following guests : Mr. Beckford (Great Northern Railway), Mr.W.H J. Jenkins (solicitor), Mr. R. Wood, and Mr. Lengbottom (London and North-Western Reilway), Mr. Thompson (Midland Rsil way), Mr. Abdy (Great Weston Railway), Mr Gibbons (Groat Central Railway), and Mr. Orawbv. At Southport, the agent for that town, Mr. Phillieps,joined the party. A start was made from Warrington at 7.45 from the Centtal Station, and after an expeditious run Southport was reached about 9 o'clock. With four hours to spare each person bad time for a good look at the pretty watering-place. Perhaps a rather shorter stay at Southport would have beea more to the general satis- faction and not make such a break in the day'a pro- ceedings, but this is quite a small thing in com- parison with the enjoyable nature of the trip. At one o'clock the excursionists embarked on the" Queen of the North," the finest of the steamers plying between Southport and Blackpeci. The calmness of the water was such to make the sail a pleasure to the most ticklish. In an hew Blackpool was reached and during ths three hours that remained the places of amusement, the promenede, and the shore were well patronised. The same veseel conveyed the party back to Seuthport which was reached soon after 6 o'clock. About 40 of the heads of departments and guests sat down to an excellent dinner at toe Prince of Wales Hotel, when the usual patriotic and loyal toasts were honoured. The toast of "Success to the firm of Peter Walker and Son," was naturally received with great heartiness. At 9.30 the special train left Lord-street Station and eonveyed the party to Warrington in excellent time. A noticeable feature of the excursion was the order and quietness maintained, there briing not the least sernbtance to rowdyism, and yet all had enjoyed themselves to the full in their own particular way.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
JULY 15th, 1893.
FRANKNESS and clearness on the Ths Liberal subject of the Liberal leadership Leadership. have become essential. There are hints and whispers of all kinds feting about, in
% way to create the impression that something.

striking is going on, with the assent of promin- ent members of tha Front Opposition Bench. We have been dispo3ed to regard them as misleading as sectional, and as indicating hopes rather than intentions. But there 5s some kind of aye- t" ill their promulgation, and they tend to be- 7:r" raore definite after a period of denials and l'aations. Some very precise statements are ,-("' being circulated, and hence it may be impor- 'ant to make one or two poidts quite clear. The 61'4 point we wish to put beyond all Possibility o:: doubt is this—that nacre in- trig" Must not be allowed to settle this question. We have had enough of that alr cat% Existing difficulties are due to the suc- cessful intrigue of a few years ago, which deprived Sir WILLIAM Illuconar of his well-earned reward. Tho matter is too import.mt to be settled by a few w:repullers, or a group of men sitting roiled a dinner-table. The whole party must have a hand in the selection, if that be the te:m which it la permissible to use. The second point is that arlY hurried action is not required, nor at present is there any reason for raising the point in an aelits form. Seine very sanguine parsons imagine that, With a leader, to whom all sections the party were attached, there would .„‘,.(3 a series of full-dress debates in the ucnise of Commons on :rotes of no confidence, la which the Government would suffer urn- Mensely. They even depict a more striking reaction in the country as likely to follow seine- thing which they but dimly describe. On the first, it may be said that the voting power of the k.tov3rament would 110th alt Tar, and it is al:nost Prom iture to sketch alternative policies in for&ln BZICI home affairs. Oa the second, it is clear that the Liberals in the country are not gravely dis- satisfied with the pre;sent state el afftirs, and the Polls show that the ve:red question as to who shall lead hereafter lfas no effect. Polls are improved and seats are won when the Liberal party is des- cribed as being in a most chaotic and deplorable condition. From these facts it may be logically inferred that the urgency of any change is not felt The general election will find it im- Portant for the country to know who Will be Premier in the event of a Libm!al majority being formed, as seems very probable. Many things may happen before then. There Might, it is quite conceivable, be a rearrange- runt of parties. There might be some large Paraonal chanqes. There may be a goad many 11-tr questions arising. Aslumin,g that the :,133rals would like to know definitely under k-"138e banner they are fighting, the time for that 12°Wledge is not yet. We must wait awhile. In " meantime the fighting in the Commons could not be in betterhands,and could not be more active Without being productive of greater unity, loyalty, and rallying power on the side of the Unionists. The Party as a whole, makes no sign of discontent with this policy of waiting, and the party as a whole must govern its affairs. Irresponsible statements about what exists, or what ougnt to be done, or What defects are 890 a here and there, are simply doing mischief. We cannot get back to office and Power by an intrigue in which some of the Scotch Liberals are leading spirits. That being settled, our councils are wise and prudent.

IN some of the prefiguring state- Inde ty. A War ments about the coming peace mai between Spain and the United states there are references to an indemnity as if tt were the most natural thing in the world. It is the very reverse, because it is quite a modem in- novation, and there are only a few cases in which It has been exacted. Russia imposed one upon Turkey, following the German precedent of 1870, and then Japan obtained the like money payment from China. France was the aggressor in the case qarmany, and hones the indemnity seemed fair eatwugh. But Russia was the aggressor in the war for Bulgaria, and Japan was the aggressor in the case of the war with China. Greece also paid an indemnity to Turkey, and was the aggressor. We may take it, therefore, that precedents support a money Payment whether the aggressor wins or is de- feated. In the case of Spain we have the aggres- sor calling for the expenses of the war to be paid hY the defeated party. There is the question of territorial compensation to be considered. France f°st Alsace-Lorraine, and still she had to pay a tlg indemnity. Turkey lost Bulgaria and East ktoureelia, as well as a part of Armenia, and terri- tory on her Caucasian frontier. China lest For- Inosa, which was, after all, but a poor compensa- tinn for Japan, apart from the indemnity of thirty zn. (Mous. Greece lost a strip of land In Thessaly Ih addition to the money payment. If, then, -4114erica were to demand from Spain an indeca- 41tY, whilst taking from her several islands also, tts would be all in h3r favour. Yet, if be any large territorial acquisitions, not seem fair to a poor country like
P"celenl
WOUld

Spain, already embarrassed in her finances, to impose upon her a large pecuniary sacrifice. If America wrests from her Cuba, Porto Rico, the Ladrones, and the Philippine Islands, she ought to consider herself amply repaid. The answer will most ikely be that some of these islands will be handed over to their inhabitants, and not become American Colonies. That, is however, another point in the conditions of peace of a disputable and undecided nature, concerning which there cannot be much clear discussion at present. We are told that America will retain Porto Rico as a guarantee for any indemnity that may be exacted. If this be so we may just as well make up our minds that the indemnity will never be paid. We do not see how Spain can pay any indemnity whatever. The state of her foreign debt and her internal condition do not admit of this kind of satisfaction. The same was said of Greece, and yet Greece was en- abled to arrange her debts and pay an indemnity as well. Why should not this be also possible in the case of Spain P There is no easy answer to this question. The peace must be an international arrangement, and when the Powers are assisting in the restoration of peace they may just as well attend to Spain's financial condition and place it upon a more satisfactory basis, if it can be done. It is clear that the other creditors of Spain must be heard when it .is proposed to exact from her several millions of money to reimburse Amerlca for what she has spent, and it is passible that con- ditions may be settled which will permanently benefit Spain and her foreign creditors. Looking all round in this way, it may be a good thing that Spain should have to pay,but the burden will have .co be adjusted to the back which has to bear it.

I Probably both parties feel some measure of satisfaction at the result of the Gravesend election. The Conservatives have succeeded in retaining the seat, and the Liberals have polled a larger number general election, 1187, to one of 417 of votes than ever before and reduced the majority aaftttehrea very brief campaign. We hardly need point, tsignificance of these figures, and we are sure u thethat the result of this election can be but a o small disappointment to the most advanced and enthusiastic opponent of the Governme,t. Grave- send was almost hopeless from the commencement, and the Liberals of that town have accoitted themselves in a fashion which cannot but contri- bute to:the spirit of unrest which afflicts the party in power. Each bye-election tells the same tale, either by the strident voice of victory or by the more subdued, but scarcely less jubilant cry of a moraltriumPh.

There is plainly very keen competition in naval ship-building between France and Russia on the one side and England on the other and from what we can learn it is the intention of the two first named powers to rival Britain's strength and may-be dispute her maritime supremacy. All this is very troublesome, and no doubt annoying to the Admiralty, who are re- sponsible for themaintenance of the superiority at sea which it has been for centuries an English- man's privilege to boast about. M. Lockroy, the prime mover in the present abnormal French naval activity, has so to speak, shown his hand and this has happened, fortunately, before Mr. Goschen has brought forward his supple- mentary naval estimates. M. Lockroy's scheme contemplates the addition of 220 vessels, of all kinds to the French navy within the next eight years, and an endeavour is to be made to complete this huge programme of extensions in three years less than the estimated or allotted period of time. The whole five or eight years' pro- gramme in France represents the enormous sum of 32 millions for new ships, cruisers, and torpcdo boats alone, and to this will be added the cost of new coaling stations, the fortifying of both old and new owes, •the extension of dockyards, and the provid!ng of the other requi.7e- Ineats ut a great fleet. With all thi.. before him Mr. Goschen will require to put on his thinking-cap, and not cease wearing it for i some time. It s clear that the enterprise of the French and Russians—for the latter have been rapidly increasing their sea forces of late years— caonot be treated with contempt or indifference. We have colossal interests to maintain, and our strength must be Titanic to saeguard those in- terests. No one will appreciate this more readily than the First Lord of the Admiralty, and his pro- posals for coping with the difficulty will be studied with interest when forthcoming. Few people have any inkling as to their nature, and it is very pro- bable that M. Lockroy's scheme may cause their immediate revision and supplementation.

But after all is said and done this competitive construction of navies is an insane procedure. Here we have all the great powers, at peace with each other, and yet watching jealously lest one should steal a march over another in the compara- tively small matter of building engines of war and destruction. As things at present exist there ap- pears no likelihood or possibility of a finality ever ' being arrived at. And yet this enormous expen- diture on the building and maintaining of battle- ships cannot go on for ever. In time the " waste of waters " will become literally overrun with vessels of war playing the cat and mous* game in times of peace, and following out a plan of mutual extermination during the progress of war. Before that extreme conditiOn of things obtains however, SDMO method of arbitration in disputes will be in yogi'', though the probability of it seems at the present time almost as remote and the nature of it almost as obscure,as it did at the dawn of civiliza- tion.

The entente cordiale between this country and America is one of the topics of the hour, and everything with a fresh bearing upon it, or con- nected with it, is interesting to the newspaper- perusing public. There has been published this week a document of unique interest, in the shape of a letter penned by Mr. G;adston ein 1880. Two sentences in this letter, which was addressed to the Right Hon. gentleman's American publishers, are remarkable in the light of current events. "And again" says Mr. Gladstone, "I have a further pleasure in becoming, in however humble a degree, a vehicle of English thought to the American mind. The union between the coun- tries is close, and is likely to grow closer still. Honour to all those who seek to corroborate the bond !" The language is n4ble, and expresses better than anything else which could be written at the present time, the sacredness of the bond which unites the two great English speaking nations of the earth. Lord Rosebery, too, has given utterance to opinions on "The English speaking Brotherhood," which have likewise a peculiar interest, as they afford the opportunity of 'placing side by side the expressions of two great statesmen, and both erstwhile Liberal Pm-niers. On Thursday he said that a good understanding between the British and American races was fraught with the best destinies of mankind. The rapprochement between the two countries needs only to be projected on disinterested lines to be- come an accomplished fact.

_ The National and Liberal memorials to the late Mr. Gladstone were both advanced a step at meet- ings of the separate committees on Wednesday. There seems to be no likelihood of the schemes clashing, and there is no reason why both shod d not adequately represent the feelings and senti- ment of the late Mr. Gladstone's admirers. The Executive Committee which is dealing with the National memorial schema have agreed that their first duty is to endeavour to establish a memorial to Mr. Gladstone which shall be personal to him and shared in by all parts of the United Kingdom and they propose in the first place to offer to under- take, with local eo-operation and support, the erec- tion of a monumental or other memorial as may hereafter be decided in the capitals of Ragland, Scotland, and Ireland, and also at Rewarder'.

Liberals in council at the National Liberal Club have decided to raise a fund for obtaining the best procurable statue of Mr. Gladstone for erection within the precincts of the Palace at Westminster, and to avoid any appearance of competition with the national memorial, and to ensure that the funds shall be subscribed by the largest possible number of Mr. Gladstone's adherents, contribu- tions shall range in amount from a penny to a pound. One very reassuring feature of both pro- posed memorials it" that there is not likely to be any difficulty with regard to funds. Most influ- ential support is being given to each scheme, and the phenomenal outburst of sentiment which followed the death of the groat statesman pre- cludes any fear of a half-hearted response to the appeal for subscriptions.

For a long number of years Lynam Cross has been a place of considerable local interest, and visitors to the village rarely return without having inspected the "historic pile." At the present time it is being renovated,—and much to its dlsadvan- tags from an aesthetic point of view. Blocks o brand new stone have been sandwiched between those which have stood for generations ; the capi- tals have been replaced with new ones of a differ- ent design; and altogether the Cross now presents the appe trance of an ugly piece of patchwork. The stocks still retain their primitive aspect, but after what has taken place in connection with the Cross, we may awake some morning to find that they have been replaced with more highly-finished timber. The work of renovation may have been undertaken with the best intentions, but it would almost have been batter to see the Cross in ruins than that the present vandalism should have been perpetrated.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, J ULY 15, IS9B
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, J ULY 15, IS9B
A SUICIDE'S EXTIttk.ORDINA.ItY
LETTER.

Oa Friday, at the Widnes Accident Hospital, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest upon the bad," of William Stacey, aged 18, who on the previous day hanged him- self in Mathieson's Work'. Mr. D. Lewis was the fore- man of the jury, and Sergeant Smith represented the police.—Mary Ann Stacey, mother oC the deceased, gave evidence of identification, and George Baguley, fitter, of I the discovery of the body hanging to the beam by means of a rope round the neck. --P.C. Guinness said he cut the deceased's bads, down, and handed in the follnwing letter, received from Mr. Whitley (the manager of the Works) : " Dear Mother,-1 am very sorry that I have to com- mit this rash act, but it cannot be helped. I have got my senses when I write this down, and they have no need to say that it was done while temporarily insane. There is no insanity whatever. Good-bye, dear sisters and brothers, good-bye dear mother,and God bless you. I must new leave this woqd of sorrows,se good-bye and God bless everybody."—Tce Coroner remarked that in some cases people had some great sorrow which they did not disclose to the outside world. There were a numter of people who would appear to have a most cheerful demeanour, and yet be burdened down with a great deal of trouble, either in private life or otherwise. There was,however,not even a suggestion that anything was troubling the deceased in this case.—After a few minutes' deliberation the jury retarned a verdict ef " Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

div.head: BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO.'S • AN NIVE RSA RT.
div.p: BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO.'S • AN NIVE RSA RT.
FETE AT WINNINGTON PARK.

A sight perhaps unique in its way was witnessed ao Winnington Park, Northwich, on Saturday, when some 12,000 people assembled to celebrate the 25ch anniver- sary of the feuneing of tho Winnington Alkali Works by the famous firm of Messrs. Brunner Mond and Co., chemical manufacturers, who now have several exten- sive establishments. Those present were almost exclu- sively the workmen employed by the firm, who brought with them their wives and children, and their grand- children too. Messrs. Brunner, Mead and Co., are known far and wide for the interest they have taken in the welfare of their employbs when inside or outside of the works. It would be hardly possible to enumerate the beneficent measures undertaken by the company on behalf of the workmen, A moclel village with model school—the en- tire cost of maint ening which has been borne by the firm—have been founded ; a large portion of the park adjoining Winnington Hall, has been given over to a recreation club, wh'ch boasts of some of the hest athle- tic and cycle tracks, bawling greens, tennis courts, Sec., , in the North of England, and which is to be reel further I improved by the erection of a pavalion and chophouse, prelented by Sir John Brunner and Dr. aloud. The firm, it may be added, was one of the filet in the king- dom to introduce the eight hours system, which is still in vogue at all their departments. The ceremony of cuttinp. the first sod far the new pavilion which is to be given by the two founders of the firm, and which is to be built on the spacious recreation , ground, wee most important proce-ding of the day, but it was only a part of the programme, and did net take long. A space of ground bad been roped off at the 'spot where the building is to be erected, and here eir John T. Brunner, and then Dr. Ludwig Mond, cut a sod, , which they carried to a barrow on spades presented to 'them as a souvenir of an interesting occasion, and as a ' slight acknowledgement of their generosity. The spades were exactly similar, and, with the exception of the necessary substitution of names, had the following in- scription :—" This spade was made by Winniegton workmen from steel made at Winnington works (by Mood's producer gas), and from oak grown in Winning- ton Park. It is presented to Dr. Ludwig Mond, F. 113., (and Sir John T. Brunner), on the occasion of cutting the first sod of the pavilion, on the 25-,h anniversary of the starting of Winniegton Works, 1873, 1898. In accepting the spade,Sir Jahn Brunner said that the 'proceedings were part of the celebration of the twenty- fifth anniversary of the startling of the works at Win- nington. In those twenty-live years had been seen, and especially seen by those who deely watched the making of history,a very happy Period in the life of the Engli3h people. During that period they had made immense progress—they bad been closing prisons all over the country they had been opening schoels all over the coon- try,they bad been opening hospitals, and last, they had been opening clubs. They of that immediate neighbour- hood had had their full share of the happiness produced by that groat progress, and he did not think it was too much for him to say that they had not only had their share,but that they had been in the very van of this pro- ' greset (Applause.) Ete might say as a proof of this that the sickness among the men attending tee works was now only half what it was when they firet began to keep a record, and that th 3 number of hijnries by ace- dent was less than half what it was 17 years ago. There In Winnington the progress had been greater, in- deed, than it had been in any other part of the country. flis friend, Dr. Mond, and nirrisolf had chorine this period had before their minds day by dav the immense responsibility that was resting upon them to look to the , welfare of those who surrounded them. They knew something of what had been done, and the work they were inaugurating that day was another step forward in the line that they had adopted in this quarter of a century. The whole of the English people nad during this period been improving in the matter of their amuse- ments. There was very much less of coarseness in the character of the amusements and they rejoiced at it. To-day the working man had precisely the same amuse- ments as well-to-do people bad a qaarter of a century age. It was with the idea of providing fer those who surrounded them that he and Dr. Mond made up their minds to present to Brunner Mond, and Co.. a pavilion, the plans of which they had studied,and which would shortly be erected upon the spot where the com- pany was then gathered. It was their hops that the club would be used, not by a limited portion of the men who were now members of the recreation club, but that it would be used by a large majority. It was their hope that in that building the men would find inmllectual and refined amusements. There would be found within its walls and under its roof a large lecture hall, billiard rooms, a reading room, and all the accommodation that was required for the purposes of the club. It was in the hope that the club would be a pleasure and a been to everyone present that he would proceed to cut the first sod as a preparation for the erection. (Applause). In accepting a spade handed to him by Mr. Green- ough, on behalf of the workmen, Dr. Ludwig Mond _ _

, Made a bri4 speech. Various votes of thanks w3re then passed, and a I)" gramme of amusements and sports was prJceeded With until eight o'cl:,ck in the evening, on the cricket ground the paddock, and another portion of the grounds. A number of large tents had been erected, where tea was dispensed, and 2,500 children were given mugs bearing portraits of Sir .r...hn &armor and Dr. Mond, The arrangements for the fete were necessarily elaborate, aod even included a tent for lost children, and an ambulance tent in case of accident. They were carried out by committees haying at their head Messrs. T. A. Johnson, J. I. Watts, C. Humphrey (Winnington), W. A. Richards (Sandnach), and Mr. 03 .vald Brock (Winning- ton), honorary secretary. In addition, of course. there were many other workers. and the proceedings were car- ried out very satisfactorily.

div.head: ENJYYMENT ALL ROUND:

On Wednesday afternoon several delightful trips were indulged in by HOalf/ of our neighbours. The S. Mr. William Henry big,titfoot, who tor the past seven years has been carrying on business as pawnbroker and Fastener, at Runco-n, died very suddenly at his residence at Helsby on Friday nigut. Though for S9MO time he was a great sufferer front Bright's disease, his end came unexpectedly. He had spent the day at New Brighton, and almost immediately on his arrival home he expired in his chair. The news came as a surprise to his many Runcorn friendc, as ho was only a few days prev.ously amongst them. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon at St. S...mes' Cemetery, Liverpool. P.S. PIIESENTAT'ON TO A WIHNES OFFICIAL. On Tuesday afternoon, at Widnes Town Hall, the Mayor (Alderman Wareing) presided over a gathering of the officials of the corporation, when a massive marble timepiece was presented to Mr. Samuel Hoyle, borough accountant, by his fellow officials and the members of his staff, on the completion of 21 years' service, as a mark of their personal friendship and high regard. div.head: S ED WARD S CA.T HOL IC MISSION.
div.p: S ED WARD S CA.T HOL IC MISSION.
SERMON BY THE REV. CANON CRAVVLEY.

On Sunday last the pulpit at St. Edward's Catholic Mission, Runcorn, was occupied by the Very Rev. einem Crawley Of Sale), who preached two eloquent sermons, on behalf of the Catholic Mission at Weston to fair congregations. In the morning he spoke upon the worilr " What more cou.d I have done for My people than I have done ?" What was there, said the preacher that they could have asked of God, that He had not given them already. They had been made for a great end— even for Himself. They were to enjoy this world inno- cently, not clinging to the ideas of the world; and thus prepare themselves to enjoy the hereafter. Jesus Christ had come into the world and suffered a most Ignominious death that a way of Salvation might be opened for them. Could they hays asked or conceived such a manner of redemption ? Healing with what people outside the Catholic pale called transubstantiation, Canon Crawley asked why was it their foes always attacked them upon their belief ; and people outside the Catholic faith, when they wanted to know anythinz about latholics—or as they called theist " Roman ttholics "—always went for that iaformation to the Attackers ? They, who were not of the Catholic fold knew that their blessed Lord took the bread into His hands and said' This is My bedy " and that " This is My blood" was the eepression used commanding the wine to be taken. If it was intended that the bread and wine were to be used " I`.l My tody "and " is My blood "it had lei-.en argued that there were from 40 to 70 words in the language the; could be used to denote that. Therefore, to them it was clear and plain that the actual change took place, and that as the priest pro- nounced the words ot consecration what had been bread was changed into the body of the Lord, and the wine was changed into His blood. This was dine be- cause the Lord cams to stay with them ; be with them ; reside with them. He was actually in that house, so hmutifully spoken of as the House of Gad. Finally the preacher exhorted then to be strong in their faith, of which they had every reason to be proud.—ln the even- ing he dealt with tho sacrament of the confession every part of which would sema strange to the outsider,—to the unbeliever. The Catholic church was performing, and had been pawn:dug its duty whilst others were neelscting it. Many of the people who ridiculed the idea of the confessional were Church of England ; but if they looked in their prayer hooks they would be! _ _ .

, prised upon turning to the" Visitation Of the Sick" to see that they too believed in it. They had the power to forgive sins—if they were Catholic priests, but others had not because they had not received the direct authority. "Whatsoever sins ye loose on earth, shall be loosed ; and whatsoever sins ye bind ; shall be bound " were the words of their own- , bless(rd Lord. They (the Catholic priests) were accused of having a fixed scale ranging from 2s 61 to lOs 63, or something of that sort, of fees for the confession, and that a man could pay his price and go absolved. But that was not so. If it were, the priests would be the richest people in the world; whereas they were the poor- est. If he himself had received only so much as 6.1 for ' every confescion he had had during his time as a con- :essor, he would now be a remarkably rich man. The speaker dealt with the number of Church of England ministera who held the same belief as they did. Speak- ing of the Mission at Weston, for which their alms were asked that day, he said he was sorry to hear that it was a drain upon the mission at Runcorn; but it spoke well for their charity and self-denial that they se ably kept it in the manner they did.—The musical portion of the service which included Farmer's Mass in 13 fiat was rendered in a most pleasing manner, and reflected great credit upon Mr. IlOckery, the able conductor of the choir. Mrs. Stancliffs, Rogent-street was the able accompanis:. The Altar had been tastefully decorated by Miss Gore with choice fl,wera,

div.p: WESI 011.
NEGLECT OF CHILDREN-AN UNTIDY HOUSE.

On Monday, before Messrs. F. J. Norman and W. Timmins at the Police Court, Runcorn, William Hares, and Sarah Hares, man and wife, late el Widnes, but now residing at Weston, were summoned at the instance of Inspseator McAteer (of the N.S.P.C.C.), for neg- lecting their five children, aged respectively : Frances, 22 pears ; William Henry 8 ; Raphael 12 ; Joseph 6 ; and Annie (a baby in arms) aged five years. Mr. A. Browne, (solicitor) Warrington, conducted the case for the &sciety ; whilst the defendant's conducted their own case. ! Evidence was given by Inspectator McAteer of visit- ing the defendant's house, in company with Police-con- stable Wylie, and of the filthy state in which it was discovered to be. There was scarcely any furniture or clothiieg in the house. The eldest daughter (who had ,an illigitimate child) slept upon what would appear to be the frame work of an old sofa, upon which was stretched a sack of chaff. Upstairs ths children slept without any covering whatever, and there was an accumulation of filth. Upon examining the children they were found to he in a very filthy and ill-clothed condition though they were fairly nourished. The husband received about 311 to 313 61., a week and gave it to his wire and they had also a !nail lo lgiag with them, who paid about 12 s a week. of the nameo Jimmy Caution. P.C. Wylie corrobarAted the previous witness and said the defendants attention was callcd to the state of the tt3use and children, and the in3pctor said hi would take proceedings against them. Sarah hares (the wife) said that the evidence wee not tru,... Her house and children were clean enough for her. They had plenty of food in the house, and at the time the inspector came in they were frying some mut- ton chop'. It was not true that there was only a pound of bread in the house.—ln cross-examination : See ad- mitted receiving 31s a weak from her husband, and also Ale was paid by the lodger 121, 84, Ss, 4s, se, and 34 61. respectively for the week's ha stayed with her. She was not in the habit of getting any drink. Louisa Taylor, Weston. called for the defence. said ' she always considered that the defendants house was clean, but she had not been upstairs only in the kitchen She was forced to admit, however, that she considered that with Co much money coming in it ought to better ' kept and furnished.—Cross examined: She did not know that the defendant got any beer. She thought the children were all right; so long as they were healthy, she did not mind what they had on, William Hares (the father) was visibly affected, and showed great reluctance in going into the box. He gave evidence of supplying his wife with all the money he earned, which was 53 31 a shift about 31s 61 a week. . He had been in regular work for the last thnte months

and never lost any time. After some deliberation the Bench slid they had de- cided to adjourn the Me against the father (William Bares) for a month and see how matters would go on ; but with regard to Mrs. Hares (who had been heard to remark to her husband, during the hearing of the case "Don't cry, we'll get drunk when we get outside")---She would have to go prison for 14 days.—lavector McAtm was asked to report upon the case at the end of a mouth, which he promised to do.

div.head: NEWTON RA.CES.
div.p: NEWTON RA.CES.
SOME OF fHE RESULTS.

Contrary to expectation, Newtsn Races were again held on Newton Race Course on Tuesday and Wednee day, owing, it is said, to the buildings at Haydock Park not being completed. Only short notice was given through the medium of the sporting press but there was, nevertheless, a large gathering of press, sporting fraternity on both days. The Viaduct Works closed on Tuesday at noon until Thursday morning, but Messrs. Vicars' and Slee did not close until Wednesday at noon. As usual there was a large number of plain clothes constables on and about the race course,and they were succeisful in making a fairly good haul of law breakers. The following are the cases ke. which were dealt with at a special court held at the Earlestown Police Station on Tuesday evening by Colonel Wood and Mr. C. B. F.Borron. Box AND Dics.—Ellen Craig pleaded guilty to playing a game of chance with box and dice.— A plain clothes Constable proved the charge, and prisoner was fined 10s. and costs. THE THREE CARD TRlCE.—Michael Black and John Kenny were charged with gaming on the Newton race course with the ehree card trick.—They both admitted their guilt, and were fined 101 and costs each. Summons CIARACTERS.—George Thompson, and John Walsh, were charged with being suspected persons and frequenting Newton races with intent to commit a felony.—They both pleaded not guilty, and Thompson expressed his indignation at being brought there en such a charge.—A constable said that about a quarter past four, he was accompanied by Constable Choriton,in plain clothes in the fifteen shilling ring on the race course, and from something said to them they followed the two men about for ten minutes—and saw them go amoneedifferent crowds of persons, and they saw Walsh put his hand in a man's pocket.—Thompson on being asked if he had any question to put, expressed ignor. ance of the charge upon which he was arraigned and seemed to think he was badly used.—Walsh had no questions to ask.—Another constable said he was in company with the previous witness, and from what Detective Kemaston of the London and North Western Railway Company said to him, they followed and watched both the prisoners for a short time, and he saw Walsh put his hand in another man's pocket.—Thomp- son said he could not ask the officer anything. All he could say was the offieer was not speaking the truth.— Detective Kynaston said he was in company with Detec- tive Jones on the race course and saw the two men in custody in the big ring. They, with another man hustled a gentleman and took something from him, but he could not say what it was, He communicated with the two previous witnesses and they saw them afterwards in various parts of the ring. The gentleman referred to said he had lost a pocket book containing cheques and notes to the value of £2oo.—Thompson said hecould ' get evidence of his respectability arid Walsh said he really did not know what he was locked up for, as he was standing with his hands in his pockets watching a fight when he was arrested.—Detective Jones corrobor- ated the previous witness.—Both prisoners were fined 20s. and costs each. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Frank Howard was charged with being drunk and disorderly and committing a breach of the peace.—Sergeant Crinkshank said the prisoner and about nine other men were in the Rains 'Head creating a disturbance and the prisoner was using sticks, and witness saw him strike the waitres. Prisoner said it was not his fault that it occurred. Ile went into the Rarn'e Head, and put down sixpence for three drinks, but only receiving two, he asked for an- other, wen the manaeer said he had had three and when he insisted that he had not, and asked for his change the manager jumped over the counter and put him out. He was bound over in £5 to keep the peace for 8 months and pay the costs. SHARP SENTENCE ON A TRICISTER.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Colonel Wood (in the chair), and Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Edward Lloyd was charged with gaming by means of the three card trick at Newton on the 13th, July.—Mr. Longton. who appeared for the defendant, pleaded not guilty.—P.C. ICooper said he was on duty en the day in question in the is. enclosure. At about 3.30 be saw the defendant in company with many others. They had a stool on which they were playing the game. He saw 30s. pass from one man. When they saw him they ran away. but he followed and caught the defendant.—By Mr. Loneton : The defendant was shuffling the cards and there were about 200 people present. Longton for the defence enegested that with such a lot of persons present the officer had mistaken the man.—The bench sent the defendant to prison for two months.

div.head: FRODSIIAM.
div.p: FRODSIIAM.

VALrE OF PROYERTY.—On Wednesday at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham, Messrs. Churton, Elphic and Co., held a most successful property sale, some of the prices realised being at the rate of £324 per acre. TREATS.—Tbe Union Church Sunday School scholars enjoyed their annual trip to Vale Royal, on Wednesday. The journey vra9 made by special steamer up the Weaver.—The infants of Miss Crosfield's Sunday school were entertained to tea upon the hills,and a most enjoy- able afternoon was speat in sports and gambols, by all the little ones who were left out of the treat last week. RESIGNATION OF TEE OVERTON BCHOOLMASTER.-Mr.J. Pollard having resigned the post of headmaster of the boys' school, Overton, MeLawrenee Magerison (who has been acting as deputy) WRP a pprilf.ted to the vacancy. —Oa Tuesday °riffling, at a envying prelided over by the Rev. 11. B. Blogg (vicar), a committee was ap- painted to promote a testimonial showing the ti 2rta Of the old scholars for Mr. Pollard's faithful work,extending over a period of forty-fonr years. VOLUNTEER CHURCIE PARADE.-03 Sunday the" I" Company (Feodsham), of the second Earl of Chester's V. 8., held their annual church parade. The weather was delightful and a record attendance established. The c ,mpany matched from their headquarters to the Parish Church where a special service was held. The officers on parade included :—Major Harrison (in command), Lieutenant Burton (Frodsham). Colonel Ashton, Captain G. F. Ashton, and Lieutenant J. L. Maurice (Rancorn). —The men were highly complimented upon their general appearance whilst on parade by Major Harrison. —On Sunday nest they will proceed to iiirkdale (South- port) for their annual encampment. BICYCLE ACCIDENT.—On Sunday, a bicycle accident that might have had more serious results, occurred at Frodehamt Bridge. As two Warrington cyclists were riding a tandem across the bridge they observed an old man (Mr. Connolly) in the road, and rang their bell and shouted. Mr. Connolly. (who is about 70 years of age), howeverthecame dumfounded and instead of getting out of the way ran right into the track of the tandem and was kaocked down, Maitainiug, severe iojaries. Dr. Bur- ton was soon in attendance, but it was not until about an bout afterwards that Mr. Connolly regained con- sciousness. One of the Cyclists WAR False severely injured and advised not to proceed on his jaurney until Some other means of locomotion could be weaned.
HALTON.

Tam LADIES' CLun.—ln accorciancri with a"cient cue torn the Haltafa Ladies' Club celebrated their 82nd annf— versary.on Monday. Assembling at Halton Castel Hotel, the members walked in precession through the village, being clad in their distinctive shawls and regalia.and on to the Parish Cnurch and p irticipated in a special ser- vice conducted by the Rev. G. D. Wray (vicar), assisted by the Rev. S. Wilkinson (vicar of Timperley). After the service the members partook of an excellent tea pro- vidnd on the Castle grounds. and in the evening a pro- gramme of dance music was rendered by the Weston band,and the dancing on the green was thoroughly en- joyed by a large nurnoer of friends.—A pyrotechniscdrissi play and illumina,tions brought the proceedings to a close. Amongst those preseat were :—Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. G. D. Wray, Mrs. Wray, ibriire. J. H. Gamon and Thomas Wright (trusteez), Mr. Percy R. Wright (ee tarv), k.—The balance sheet for the year showed that £96 91. was disburse:l in sick payments, £lO in funeral meney, and £34 for medical attendants. The subscrip- tions nf urn:than amounted to £l4B 3i. Bi. The total worth of thfi society on D.,cernher 31st, 1897, was shown to be £1,548 17s. 7d.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

ROBBIRT FROM TIM WARRINMTON CRICKET PAVILION. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday morning, before Mr. F. Meeks and other magistrates. three youths, named Thomas and Percy Quinn, 4, Dal- lam-lane, and John Finnigan, 37, Town-hill, were charged with stealing from the Arpley Cricket Pavilion, between 9.45 on Saturday night and one o'clock on Mon- day morning, a number of articles, including three tennis balls and a packet of cigars, the property of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club.—Prisoners pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable said the prisoners were originally charged with breaking and entering the cricket pavilion and stealing articles, but it wag thoueht advieable to reduce the charge, so that the court might have jurisdic- tion. At ten minutes to twelve on Sunday night P.S. Hollingsworth was in Wilderspool.road,near the railway crossing,when he heard some persons on the iron bridge. He went there, and saw the priaoners in a recess in the bridge. They were in a shocking state of drunkenness. I He questioned them as to where they got the drink from and they marls rambling statements. One rif them said i a man belonging to Arpley cricket ground gave them I drink and cigars. The boys were taken to thel Police Station. They were in such a C9O- - that emetics bad to be given to them.' The pavilion caretaker, on examining the place after- wards, found the door of the main pavilion had been I opened, presumably by a key. The door which led from the pavilion to the refreshment her had been forced open by means of a butcher's steel, which was found there. About a pint of spirits was missing, as well as a quantity of cigarettes, cigars, spoons, lawn tennis balls, and other things. On Thomas Quinn were found tea spoons and cigarettes, on Percy Quinn tennis balls, ke., and on Finnigan, tennis balls and a packet of cigars. There was no doubt that the youths had broken the place open, and gorged themselves with spirits. They had not quite recovered yet. Percy Quinn had a bad record, and he thotteht he was the ringleader. He had been eight times before the court for thefts, and ren the last occasion he was sent to prison for fourteen days. He had been in a reformatory school for five years,and Inspector Monaghan said he was the ring- leader of a gang of thieves in Warrington. He had also been birched three times. Thomas Quinn had been be- fore the court three times for theft, and had served one day's imprisonment. There was nothing against Finni- gan.—The magistrates ordered Finnigan to be kept in the cells for three days and Thomas Quinn was sent to gaol for two months and Percy Quinn for three months. 58R10179 CHARGH AGAINST • WARRINGTON MAN—RRSI7LT Or A QUARREL. At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday morn- ing, before Mr. John Faircleugh (in the chair) and Meters. Gedeee and Birchall,John Shaw, 55, Wellington. street, was summoned with inflic'ing grievous bodily harm on Joseph Dooley, in a stable at Howley on Mon• day night.—The Chief Constable applied for a week's remand. He said the prisoner was working on Monday for Mr. John Clifton Lunt, who carries on business in Mowley-lane as an off-beer seller. Mr. Lunt had a hay field in Howley Meadows, and prisoner was employed there. Serno of the mem who had assisted in the hayfield had received no money fer their services, and Mr. Lunt gave them a little beer in the stab!e. While there a dis- Cll3SiOn arose between the men, and Dioley, who was reputed to be of a very quarrelsome and violent disposi- tion began to rail at prisoner and provoke him, Finally Dooley took off his cap,and shook it in prisoner's face. Prisoner told him to take it away, but he would not. Prisoner thereupon knocked it away, when Dooley sprang at his throat. Ihisoner, in sheer self-defence, struck out with his ssts,hitting Dooley on the eye a blow which.unfortusately,caused Dooley to fall back,striking his bead on the setts. He was not then anconscious,but after being taken home became unconscious. His con- dition became so serious that Dr. Braid's was called in, We gave information to the police, and in view of the pessible turn the case might take he (the Chief Con- stable) deemed it advisable to have the prisoner in cus- tody,as much for his own protection in the matter as to further the ends or justice. Supposing the worst hap- pened,and Deoley regained consciousness before death, his statement, which would be taken in prisoner's pro sence would probably exonerate him from blame.—Pri- soner,who had nothing to say, was remanded until the 19th instant. PanvencE OF SIIICIDII TO FRIGHTEN A HUSBAND. At the Warrineten Borough Police Court on Wednes- day, beers Mr. John Faircleugh and other magistrates, Pauline Oaitram, married woman, living at 31, Liver- pool-road, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Liverpool-road at half-past eleven on Tuesday night.—The Chief Constable said that the magistrates would observe that the charge of drunkenness was written over a aharge of attempted suicide. The latter charge had been withdrawn because the attempt at suicide was a very half-hearted affair, as would be seen later on. The prisoner's husband was a elasa maker,and a respectable man. Prisoner had been drinking for some sonsiderable time. She bad appeared before the Innis tratee on 28 occasions, and her habits lately had been more intemperate than usual. On Tuesday afternoon she was away from her home, and did not return until eleven o'clock. Shortly before her return Police Cen- stable Smith heard a great disturbance going on in Leicester-street, and en going there be found a crowd of about 200 people, in the midst of whom was the Prisoner, who was using most abominable language. The constable endeavoured to take her home, but she refused to go. Finally her husband came oa the scene and took her home. When she was in the house her husband asked her about some money which Isad been in a drawer. She told her daughter to go and look in the drawer for it, but she returned saying she could not find any. Prisoner said she would find it. She did not however, but came across a razor. She said They shall not take inc; I shall not be locked up." and drew the razor across her throat. The result wee, however, only a mere scratch, and he (the Chief Constable) thought the woman had only made a pretence to cut her throat so that she might frighten her husband. He took the razor from her, but was so alarmed that he called in a policeman, and prisoner was taken to the Police Station. Prisoner had been repeatedly sent to gaol with- oUt the option of a fine, and he suggested that she should be sent to gaol for the present offenee.—The enagietrates committed priboner to gaol for a month with hard labour.

ASSAULTS AND CHLRGILS OF ASSAULTS.—Mary Turner, of 1, Howaed-street was summoned on a charge of assaulting Hannah rtephens, 44, Howard-street, on the sth July, and a cross-summons bad been issued by Turner caarging Stephens with assault. —Mrs. Stephens stated that on the date named Mrs. Turner bed been talking about witness's daughter, and on going to speak to her about it Mrs. Turner threw a lading-can fell of water at her, and also struck her on the eye with the can causing her eye to te discoloured.— Evidence in corroboration was given by Mrs. Rowlands, a neighbour, sad a little girl.—Mrs Turner denied the assadrit and splice of the provocation she had received. A witness having given evidence in corroboration, the magistrates dis- missed both cases, each party to pay their own costs.—Harry Hartiey. a butcher. of 108. Sharp street, was summoned on a charge of assaulting his wife Mary Hartley, on the 29th June —Mr. Jenkins represented the complainant, and stated that the married life of these young people had been exceed- ingly painful. He wished to modify his remarks as having regard to the time of their lives, they might reasonably hope there was a better future before them. Previous to the assault complained of arrangements had been made for the removal of the furniture belonging to the two parties In the case from the butcher's shop to a house in Percy-etreet. During the greater pert of the night preceding the 29th June. they had been engaged in removing their furniture. At this time the complainant's baby was seriously it, and he might Bay that it died this week, end was bored the previous day. The complainant arrived at the new house about 4 o clock in the morning and whilst sitting in a chair with the baby in her arms the defendant, who was under the influence of drink at the time, rushed at her with a butcher's knife in his hand and threatened to take her life. She ran into the lobby in terror and was followed by the defer,dant. The complainant was in fear of her life. The defendant afterwards threatened to do something to himself but was prevented from doing so by some friends who ook the knife from him. In doing so a man named Baldwin was cut on the leg. He (Mr. Jenkins) was Instructed to apply for a separation order.—The complainant was called and spoke of the unhappy married life she had had with the defendant. She corroborated her solicitor's statement with ref arenas to the assault, and stated that the defendant threatened her, saying he would eit ler put an end to her or an end to himself.—Hannah 11 wards also spoke in support of the complainant's ease.—The defendant stated that he was aggravated by the complainant's conduct When she got into the new house she sat down on the table and commenced to use most abusive language. He told her he did not want to have any bother,but she continued calling him and the house which caused him to get in a rage, lie admitted that he threatened her. Since he had been married the provocation he received was" something cruel."—Albert Smith stated that he assisted the defendant to remove on the night in questien. It would be tour o'clock in the morning when the complainant went to the new house. He proceeded to detail the language used by the complainant which was most abusive. She was one of the most disgrace- ful women he had known, and she was also a bad tempered women.—Questioned by Mr. Pierpoint, witness said he believed there were faults on both sides. The defendant was not a drunken man although he did take drink.—After evidence had ben given by a witness named Baldwin, the magistrates fined the defendant 10s and costs (El 53), or 14 days imprisonment. The Mayor said the magistrates could not grant a separation on the present charge. He advised the parties to live a better life together in future. " A Boo's lire."—James Graham, 25, Chorley-street. was summoned for deserting his wife Mary Graham 5, Foster-st. —Mr. Forehaw represented the de'endant. and stated that his client was thrown out of the house by his wife, He read, two excellent characters of the defendant, one from Mr. Griffiths,of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Comp my I and the other from Mr. Howard. The defendant's wife was a drunken woman, and led her husband a fearful life. He was desirous of having a separation order, and asked for the maintenance of the children, lie would also contribute to- wards his wife—The magistrates could not sea Odle' way to grant a separation order but adjourned the case for a month to see if the parties could live together again.—The defendant said it was " a dog's life with her." CIIARGE Or USING TESEATI.—Charles Spencer, a youth, living at 40. Nicholson-street, was summoned for using threats to Ann Rigby, of 20. Nicholson-street. —From the evidence it appeared that the c use arose out of defendant's treatment of a cat be'onging to the complainant. She remonstrated with him, and he then made use of a threat to em ash her face. —The defendant said he never intended to do anything of the sort, and the magistrates dismissed the case. SiTunoix.—Before Mr. Thomas Birchell (in the chair), Mr. John Fairolough and Mr J W Hayward. FREQUENTING.—Thernatt Henry Sherlock (18) last from Birkenhead was charged with frequenting in Scotland-road, with intent to commies felony. Prisoner pleaded guilty.— The bench committed prisoner to prison for seven days hard labour

AaSCONDING FROM THE WORlCl(oll9lC—Willirm Houlding, charKed with absconding and taking clothing the pro- perty of the Warrington Guardians, pleaded not guilty. The Chief Constable said the defendant had been in and out of the Workhoule ten times durng the last fifteen months. He went out on the 10th August last, dressed in Workhouse clothes and had not been aeon until July 6th. Mr. Shearer who prosecuted on behalf of the Union authorities said he was a worthless character and well-known to the police, and asked the bench to make an example of him—Defendant said he was sorry for what had happened. He had slept in a field and had been robbe3 of his sho.s. coat sal waistcoat. —lle was sent to prison for two months hard labour. A 27 Detz FATHER--Thomas Griffin pleaded guilty to leav- ing his children ehargeible to the Union.—Mr. Shearer, who prosecuted for the Union, said it was a peculiar case. The defendant had six children. His wife was sent last May to the Asylum. Since that time his children had been very much neglected. He had applied to the Union for them to take his children. He was getting about Aos. per week. He at last threw up his situation and went to she Workhouse with his children, who were in a very neglected condition. Defendant had simply made up his mind not to keep his chil- dren. —Defendant said since his wife went to the Asylum he hod had no one to look after them.—The bench sent him to prison for a month. MONDAY.—EgIfOre Mr. F. Monks (In the chair), Messrs. I Thomas Pirchall, J. W. Hayward. Samuel Wright, Councillor Shaw Green, Alderman Blackhnrst, Councillor James Smethurst.

lIIIXdra. 6 AWAY FROM THR BOROUGH.—Willianx Lowe, porter, 22. Brwood-stre.t, was charged with running away from the borough, leaving his wife and children chargeable to the Union.—Mr. Shearer who prosecuted on behalf of the Union authorities, said the defendant's wife and children were admitted to the Workhouse on the 22nd May, since that time the defendant had been away. Meantime the wife and children had left the Workhouse. Defendant returned on Saturday night, and his wife gave him in charge He had 251 a week standing wages before he went away. Defendant was sent to gaol for two months hard labour. A Vatuctous DEFENDANT.—WiIIiam Connor. fish hawker. 10. Ring-street. and Alban Stirrup. •• Soldiers Return," Pinner's-brow, were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in the Market-place on the 2nd July.— Connor did not appear.—The officer said he received in'orma- Unix on the day in question that the defendants were fighting in the Market-place. He went there. He found them and told them he would report th .rn. They said they " would hare it out. Witness then took them down to the police stotion. It was decided to issue a warrant for Connor. —Stirrup was bound over to keep the pnice for six months ' and pay the costs.—Connor now arrived in the court and said he had been unable to get before. In defence Connor intd the other defendant and some other youths had been , threatening an old m in. They had formed a circle round I the old man and after feinting with their fists and asking where would he have it " they struck him. He (Connor) Interfered and " took on "Stirrup when the officer came on the scene —The officer when asked for details threw a 1 different light on the matter.—The Chief Constable said Connor had been 39 times before the magistrates. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months and pay the costs, or in default seven days.
TUESDLY.—Before Mr. Thoroal Birehall (in the chair), CoJnoillor Shaw Green. and Mr,R..G.arnett.

THREATENING TO USE A KNlFE.—Patrick Wade was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting Ann Troy on Monday night.—Defendant pleaded not guilty —P.C. Rerldlngton maid he was on duty in Winwick-street about half-past four when he rEceived a complaint from Ann Troy. She had to run out of the !lease to escape his violence. Witness went to Saver-street. He found defendant in the middle of the street drank. He (defendant) ran at Ann Troy whets his daughter, and kicked her on the leg. He took a pocket knife out of his pocket and chased her saying he would cut her threat. Witness took him down to the police station.—lnspector Phillips corroborated as to the state of defendant. He was very drunk.—Defendant said he had had a few pints of beer and the complainant had been calling him names, but he did not strike her.—The Chief Constable : It is a very bad case chasiug a woman with a knife.—The Chairman said they were determined to mark their sense of the heinousness of that sort of thing and sent him to prison for a month. DRUNK AND Doomozat,V.— Margaret McLoughlin, a well- known character, was charged with having the previous morning been drunk and disorderly in Irlam street.—P.C. Pennington stared that the prisoner came to the Police Station in a drunken condition. She used abusive language. and he was obliged to put her into the street on four separate occasions. He eventually looked her np.—e.s. }lvens gave corroborative evidenc..—The defendant denied that she was drunk.—The Chairman : You will be sent to prison for one month hard labour.—The Prisoner' Thank you sir.
