"PENNY WlSE."—William Clarke. Devonsbire-egoare.sum- mooed for allowing his dog to be at large without a name upon its collar, pleaded guilty.—P.O. Bdwards proved the case ; he SAW the dog at large ..on the 2nd of July.—Defend ant said he had ant the name upon the dog's collar with a knife, and there were the remains of a W " and - to be seeu still.-3uperintendent Okell : The name Is to be en- graved, not cut on in that fashion.—The Chairman : We are sorry for yua, bet you see that the few pence you have saved lor engraving will have to go now.—Fined 5s including costs. —William LoTatt, Urweldiane, pleaded guilty to a Ike offence, whi th he said occurred by a mishap and which had since been rectified. and was fined 55 Inclusive of costs. STONE THROwING. THE MAGISTRATES DETERMINED TO STOP LT.—itephen Rhodes, 15, Gilbert-street.was summoned for throwing 'togas in the streets, by P.O. Gregory.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—P.O. Gregory s del they received numerous complaints about the destruotion of property by the practice, from several property owners.—A fine of five Rhillings was imposed.—Bnoek Shaw. Shaw-streat, Pis also fined 5s or seven days.for a similar offence.—Mr.Norman ex- pressed the hope that the Press would rnake a note of the manner in which the Bench were disposed to deal with all cases of stone-throwing that came before them, with a view to stamping It out. STONE-THROWING AT A RAILWAY Tharir.—Leonard Tonks, a little boy residing with his father at 13. Oak-street. was sumnamed at the instauce of Inspector Atklns(of the London and North-Western Railway Co) for throwing stones at a Railway train to the danger of the passengers, on the 24th of June.—The case for the company wts conducted by Mr. Finney. of Chester, who said that the company had no desire , to inflict great punishment upon the little boy who upon this I ea/melon had been guilty of a very great offence. At the time the stone was thrown there was a young lady looking out of the carriage window, and the affair might have had very serious results.—P.U. Kendrick gave evidence thd he was on duty in Brindley-street and saw the boy throw the stone Invo- I duced) at the train. The stone rebounded and dropped at his feet. He went up to him and said he would have to report him. The boy gave his correct name, but a wrong age an 4 address. He said he Was between II and 12.—1 n answer to the Bench the father said the boy was 8 years of age.—The boy pletded geilty.—ln answer to the Bench the fathers tid he would leave them to deal with the case. He was himself against the practice of stone throwing, and had se^eral win- dows recently broken at the Mersey Mission.—The Bench. addressing the bey, said Leonard Tooke we are sorry to see a boy of your appearance in such a position, but you did very wrong in throwing stones at the railway carriages, and you will have three strokes with the birch from Police Constable Gregory, which was a very lenient view of the case.

The fourth annual picnic of the members and friends of the Everton Liberal Association on Satur- day afternoon at Hale was attended by nearly 200 ladies and gentlemen.—Mr. Henry Jones read the following letter from Sir John Brunner, who was unable to be present :—" Dear Mr. Jones,--lt, is a great pleasure to me to hear of the energy with which you and your colleagues are conducting the affairs of the Liberal Association. There never was a time when it was more incumbent en Liberals to keep their principles before the public mind,and to make every preparation for securing the victory of those principles when next an appeal shall be made to tbe judgement of the country. The symtonas of dissatisfaction are becoming every day more ap- parent among the supporters of the Ministry. Lord Salisbury's vacillation and Mr. Chamberlain's esca- pades have excited widespread alarm and disgust, and even the strict di icipline of the Tory party al- legiance is not proof against the intolerable strait' to which it has lately been subjected. I atm glad to think that the Everton Liberals are already prepar- ing for the etruggle,and I wish that the Liberal or- ganisations throughout the country would imitate their wise example." div.head: OF A LlChni MAN.
div.p: OF A LlChni MAN.

s.- On Saturday afternoon a shocking fatality occured at tleatley Railway Station. William Read, 75 years of age, of Newffelds, Lymm, was crossing from one platform to the other to obtain a ticket I for Dunham Massey, when the train he intended I travelling by, the 4.25, came into the station, and before Read could clear the six-foot he was caught by one of the buffers of the engine and knocked under the train. He was badly mutilated by the tender box, but when the train was brought to a standstill he was found to be still alive, and was taken to the Railway Hotel, where he received immediate attention from Dr. Underwood. The case was, of course a hopeless one. The unfortunate man never regained consciousness, and died in very short time. It seems that whea he was about to cross the lines, the station-master and others on the platform sheeted to him a warning of the approach of the train, and a man who was near at hand caught hold of him and attempted forcibly to keep him back. Deceased, however, got away, and jumped down from the platform. The engine driver saw him,and immediately sounded his alarm and shut off steam. He could not bring the train to a standstill in time, with the result already re- lated. The affair was witnessed by several people, and created a very painful sensation. FARM FIRE NEAR WARRINGTON. At 3 40 on Saturday afternoon, information was , received at the Warrington Fire Brigade Station I that a fire had broken out at Oakwood Farm, occu- pied by Mr. W. Whittle, at Risles. The alarm was given, and the brigade, under the deputy superin- tendent, Mr. Frank Turner, jun , promptly tlrned out with the fire engine Major. At Padgate an, accident occurred. The vehicle was drawn by three horses, and as they were proceec:ing at a rapid rate through Padgate one of the animals stumbled and fell, and was dragged along the road for some dis- tance. The firemen quickly dismounted, released ' the unfortunate animal, which was rather seriously injured, and removed it to an adjoining stable. Mr. Turner then wired to Warrington for a veterinary surgeon. The brigade were only delayed for a few minutes. On arriving at the farm, which is the property of Messrs. 11. and R. Ain.Acough, of Orms- kirir,they found the barn, shippon, and stables were on fire and well alight, the roof having already cellapsed. A good supply of water was obtained from a pit about 200 yards distant,and the firemen with c-mimendable promptmess had two powerful jets quickly at work. In two hours the fire was extinguished. The contents of the buildings, in- cluding farm implements, some tons of straw, and several hundred sprittiag boxes, were destroyed. The damage, which is estimated at £4OO, is covered by insurance. Mr. Whittle had recently erected half-a-dozen new stacks in close proximity to the buildings, and their escape is due to the fact that the wind was blowing away from them. The origin of the fire is unknown. There was only a serYant and a little girl on the farm premises at the time, and the first alarm was given by the child, whose screams drew attention to the fire. The men were brought in from the fields, and one of them rode off immediately to Warrington for the fire brigade. The members of the brigade arrived back in Warrington at half-past seven.

div.head: LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE COUNTY ASSOCIATION. SENIOR COMPETITION, THIRD ROUND.
div.p: LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE COUNTY ASSOCIATION. SENIOR COMPETITION, THIRD ROUND.

WARRINGTON CEMETERY T. WARRINGTON SOUTII.—The meeting of these old rivals on Saturday at Croft's Bank, Urmston, aroused all the old rivalry which has marked the previous encounters which now extend over a number of years. In sporting circles the meeting has been the sole theme Of conversation and the chances of each team were discussed to such an extent that favouritism was evenly divided The first quartette. of games ended in the Man- chester-road contingent taking such a decided lead that the south players practically never recwered their position. B. Taylor crewed a surprise oy distaaceing T.Davies by fourteen shots, the most decisive win of the afternoon. J. Ashton augmented the cemetery lead by ten points, and his game with T. Locker was never in the doubt. It was a rare struggle between Q. Ball and H. Fogg, for after the game had been called 20-15 in Fogg's favour, Nall secured the jack, and ran out the , winner by a single point. The greatest surprise of the after- noon was the manner in which J Swanton disposed of T Bolton, a ding-dong game resulting, in Swanton crediting the South with their first win by two points. The next quar- tette of gnmes saw a more evenly-balaaced state of affaire,and N Shaw scored a meritorious win over A J Jones. but the advantage was lost by U Littlewood, who fell a victim to T Bridge's consistent good length woods. Herman Williams again proved his sterling worth by easily disposing of the old medalist, F Berry, and from the fourteenth end the elxug a i n „3,g South player had no chance whatever. J Shaw accounted for T Cooper, taking a decided lead and holding the issue in said keeping throughout. The Cemetery players enjoyed a Lied of 26 when the last set of players appeared on the green, and when It Bothwell defeated W Bolton by nine points, an easy victory for the Manchester-road contin- vent was proclaimed. T Hackett and it • Anderton i'ave a rare exhibition of trundling, but the Ceme- tery captain never recovered from a decided lead taken by Hackett and in the end was defeated by five points. J Gieave gained a victory over J Allison by three points, the players in a game extending over 2 ends, whilst consistent p e peeling Playern thatwinson repeatedly 8 g al by defeating T Ellison by six points. Each side w but the decisive victories gained by the Cemetery during the early games ensured thir success. The match was played with good spirit, and the referees, Metiers g, Williamson and A. Faulkner, gave every satlefsetion in discharging their onerous duties. Appended are the returns :

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHETRCITES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHETRCITES.
BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFORD,

The anniversary sermons of this chapel were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. J. F. Porteous, of Doncaster. In the afternoon the preacher delivered a powerful ser- mon to a very large audience. An anthem was also given by the choir in a very able manner. In the even- ing the p-si Leber took as his text the 21st chapter of S. John, 21st and 22nd verses " Peter seeing him saith to Jesus, Lord and what hall this man do?' Jesus saki' unto him ' If I will that he tarry till I waifs what is that to thee ? Follow thou me.' " This said he preacher was the last recorded dialogue between our Lord, Jesus Christ and that disciple who figured so prominently, and being the last recorded dialogue it was ef touching interest. Three years before by the lake Iside Jeans said to Peter " Follow me," and now at the self same spot he said "Follow me." The preacher dwelt I upon the words "Follow me." It was the duty of every one to follow our Lord Jesus Christ. Peter was in effect told not to trouble about what he could net understand, but simply to follow Jesus. This was our duty also, Things we could not understand we should not concern ourselves about but think only of the present insomuch e. it offeuteul the tu'Uto. 'Fhe preacher told a story of his student days, lie had an examination paper before him and ha had to get so many marks. Some questions were very difficult and others were easy. Hii duty was to get marks, fie solved the easy questions first and made sure of them and then he had time to think of the others after. That was our duty in every day life. More of us would come out better if we let speculation alone I and made sure of the duties we understood. When a fire occurred we at once endeavoured to put it out. We did net trouble about its origin until it had been nut out. After we could inquire how it happened. We should best lock after the future by doing our present duty and so set our children an example of faith. The preacher's sermon was eloquent and was listened to with deep in- torest by a large congregation. An anthem was given Iby the choir. The collections for the day were entirely satisfactory.

div.head: LOCAL FRIENDLY SOCIETY MEETINGS
div.p: LOCAL FRIENDLY SOCIETY MEETINGS
LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS.

On Saturday the quarterly. --riTieti-ng-Wiii;e-ii-eTrington district was held at the Shepherds by night Lodge,Lymm Temperance Hotel, under the presidency of Bro. Henry Warburton, and he was supported by Bros. William Hall (deputy-chief), James Parr, (district treasurer), Peter Edgar (district secretary), William Eckersley (trustee), and delegates representing the lodges belonging to the district. The Chairman opened the proceedings with a few appropriate words of welcome, and after the dela- , gates bad answered to the roll call, the Secretary, at the I request of the President, read the quarterly accounts of the several funds in connection with the district, which proved to be of a highly satisfactory claa.racter,and they were unanimously passed. After , a large number of new members had been passed for admission and an auditor elected, the meeting proceeded to the election of officers for the ensuing twelve months. Bro. William Hall was unanimously elected chief of the district. FOr the posi- tion of deputy chief there were four candidates. Con- siderable interest was evinced in the election, which resulted, after sonse close voting, in the appointment of Bro.F. S.Massey. Bro. Lawrence Weir and David Harris were re-elected without opposition district and book ex- aminers. The Arbitration Committee having been elected, the A.M.C. delegate (Bro. W. Eckersley) presen- t2d his report upon the proceedings of the order at their annual meeting, held in Whit-week, at Belfast. A short discussion took place upon the various subjects referred to.--On the motion ofeiro. Taylor, supported by Bros. Weir, Haley, and others, a hearty vote of thank, was passed to Bro. Eekersley for his able and exhaustive report. Bro. E:kersley suitably acknowledged threcora- pliment.—After the installation of the new officers, and before closing the meeting, the Chief-elect (William Hall) presented to Bro. S. Broady, on behalf of the members of the Shepherds by night Lodge, a handsome framed emblem of merit, for valuable services rendered to his lodge.—Bro. Hall and other members spoke in high terms of the work that Bro. Broady had performed.— Bro. Broady suitably responded. ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS.

The quarterly meetings of the Warrington District of the Ancient Order of Foresters was held at the Horse Inn, Widnes, on Saturday. The delegates present were Bros. J. J. Dennett (Court 138),Creorge Allen(Court 240) Henry James (Court 430), J. Rutter (Court 43/), W. Orrett (Court (461), and J. Holland (Court 471). The Chief Ranger, flro. W. Allen,(Court 240), presided. The District Secretary's (Bro. Llewellyn Davies) report showed that the contributions from the various courts amounted to £B2 19s, 3d., whilst the disbursements in- cluded £9O for funeral allowances. £1,501 /5s 4d. was soundly invested, and there was a balance of £1,495 15s 51. A grant was made to the Welsh Coal Distress Fund of £l. The usual votes of thanks concluded the meeting, after which the delegates eat down to a capita repast, served by Bro. John Twigg,

GENERAL NEWS.
The Duke of Argyll is writing a memoir of himself and his times.

Mr. A. Fairrie, of Liverpool, died suddenly on Tuesday evening while walking on the banks of he Dee at Chester. James Watt, a labourer, of Sprewa on, was executed at Nor- wich, on Tuesday, for the murder of his wife. A watchmaker named John Price met his death while rid- ing a bicyele on Monday nic,ht at Gresford, near Wrexham. The Duke of Cambridge on Monday opened the new Waterloo and City Electric Railway, the second of the under- ground electric systems In London. On Wednesday afternoon Taniwyn, near Colwyn Bay, the Welsh residence of Mr. Bills Lever, was practically gutted by lire. Margaret Davies, wholesale butcher. West Bromwich, was fined £ll at Rowley, on Wednesday for exposing unwhole- some meat in Cradley Heath Market. The Protestant and Catholic Missions at Shan 'King Fn have been attacked by rioters. Sir Claude Macdonald has , insisted on the immediate restoration of order in the Chin Kiang district. Thomas Jones, Hawker. belonging tn Alcawah, Was sen- tenced to death at Merionethshire Assizes. at Dongelly. on Tuesday, for the wilful murder of Mary Bruton. on a moon- tam, near Festinlog, on the sal eat of the let tdareta.

I Whilst boring for coal in he Isle of Man, in the hops of I inding a continuation of the seam th t dips towards the west at Whitehaven, there has been discovered a deposit Of rock of the highest quality.

The Rev. B. D. Cornish, minister at Eccles New road Church, Manchester. was at the conference at Line-in on Tuesday, unanimously elected president on the United Methodist tree Churches. The Exohequer returns from April Ist to July 9th show : Receipts. £27,333,130; expenditure, £32,437,870 ; balancer, £Z.736354. Corresponding period last year—Receipts, £27,057,958 ; expenditure, £30,751,138 ; btlances. £2.349.618. A train front Belfast Wised the points at the entrance to Lame Station on Wednesday morning, and a number of pas- sengers sustained injuries more or less serious. There was considerable destruction of roiling stock.

Mrs. Robert Louis Stevenson haa arrived in London. and is staving, p-obably till the end of the season, with her son and daughter-in-law, Mr. and Mrs. Lloyd Otb)rne, and her dangliter, Mrs. Strong, at No. 34, Oxford-terrace, Hyde Park. Lord Hatchery unveiled a memorial to Edmund Burks ia the parish church of Beaconsfield. flocks, on daturday. • luncheon took place afterwards, at which Lord Hotebery made a short speech. . . .

A hammermarn named Bryson is in tho custody of the Glasgow police on a charge of murdering an old woman Lamed McMillan. After a drinking bout on Saturday even- ing Bryson appears, for no reason. to have smashed the woman's head to a pulp with his boots.

Taree young men named William and George Stephenson, brothers, and Frank Malcolm hive b-en drowned while bith- ing at Deneholme, on the coast of Durham. Henry Collin- son was drowned while bathing at Scarborough on &fondly morning..

At Birmingham on Monday a local auctiunee: named David Jackson was committed for trial on a charge of fraud by run- ning the well-known racehorse Park Paid° tic at the War- wickshire Yeomanry Races as Chtrley's Aunt, and gaining an allowance of two stone. .

The humming of telegraph wires is a phenomenon which has not been sttisfactorily explained. Ills no: caused by wind, for it is heard during calms. It has been conjectural that changes of temperature, which tighten or loosen tie wires, produce the sound,

Tom Cannon, the champion wrestler, of Liverpool has ar- ranged a match with Paul Pons. the French giant wrestler. for the championship of the world. The contest between these two redoubtable foes will take place at the Evertort Football Club's ground on Saturday. the 30th inst. Mr. Angus Mackay. a well-known Irish journalist, died rather suddenly at Dublin on Tuesday from the after-effects of Influenza. The deceased was for several years connected with the" Irish Times," and was held in great estsem by his colleagues. lie leaves a widow to lament his loss. A kitten was lately brought up on an exclusively vegetable diet by a London fancily of vegetarians. The result is that it will not touch animal food and pays no attentioa ta rats or mice that are purposely permitted to run across its range of vision.

,•I lathe Divorce Division on Monday Mrs. Isabel Hamilton 'Fox, now residing with hr relations in Liverpool, obtained a decree nisi for dissolution of marriage on the ground of the Cruelty and adultery of her husbind, Dr. William Henry Piercv Fox, practising in Clapham. A despstch from Vienna says Captains Boltscheff and Noueiltsch, the former prefect of police, who were arraigned for the murder of Anna Simon. mistress of the Premier, in April, 1893, were hanged at five o'clock on Wednes day Morning in the prison at Philippopolis. The handwriting experts have won their suit for libel against H. Zola and the manager of the •• Aurora." The latter was condemned to pay a floe of 5 000 f., and M. Zola was sentenced to 16 days' Imprisonment and a fine of 2,0J0f. The plaintiffs were each awarded 3.0001. damages.

The nominations for the vacant seat at Gravesend took place on Saturday. Mr. W. Runcirnan, shipowner. Liberal, and Mr. T. H. D. Ryder. banker' Csns rvative, were duly nominated, the threatene 'iedeoeadent" 'tura of Captain ff. IL Davis not being persisted in. Eilr Edward Fry, who has been asked by the President of the Board of Trade to act 85 conciliator in the Sonth Wale coal trade dispute, commenced his work in th t c spasity on Saturday, when he had an interview with the men's repre- sentatives. The proceedings were private.

Two young pugilists, hailing from rewards and Barry, res- pectively, were the principals in a most dererrnmed prize right with bare fists, which took place near Cardiff early on Wednesday morning. After twenty-two stubborn roan& had been fought, the Barry man's seconds threw up the sponge. At the Westminster Police Court on Monday a West Bad doctor named John Lloyd Whltmarsla was charged with performing an illegal operation upon a young woman who diedin Westminster Hospital. He was remanded, and ball was refused, He strongly denied the charge when arrested.

A fire broke out early on Sunday morning in a boot shop adjoining the Balmoral Hotel, Scarborough. The hotel roof caught fire, and the guests and servauts were roused and as- sembled on the ground Fortunately, however, the spread of the flames, as far as the hotel was mammal, was Checked. but the shop was destroyed. r The Lincoln police are investigating a series of attacks with a knife upon females. On Saturday night three young women were stabbled, and three other cases had taken place previously. In each instance the wound was in the back and with regard to one or two of women their injuries are rather serious. The man by whom the wounds were inflicted who is apparently a lunatic at large, has so far es:aped arrest. Two sepoys of the sth Punjabis, while grazing goats near Jandal (India) were attacked by eight Mahatma arme4 with knives and stones. One of the sepoys was rendered insen- sible, but the other managed to mak° his way back to the camp. Troops promptly arrived oo the scene of the outrage and scoured the hills. They failed, however, to capture the offenders. - - - - -

About seven o'clock oa Wedassday whtle men were taking down a wall eighteen inches thick and fourteen feet high in the Royal Gardens of the Falace, it. suddenly fell over with a lo u I crash and buried a msn named Jahn Fuller. aged 30, of Hampt m. He was quickly taken out, but Dr. Seeger, who was summoaei, pronouaced life extinct, Several others were lojured.

Sir J. Gordon Sprigg, the Cape Premier, speaking at a meeting at Bast Loudon said the present issues were so great that he trembled at the responsibility resting upon him. The Government wanted the verdict of the people on the two following principles, viz. British suprernmy in Sonth Africa and the better representation of the people in Parliament.

- Tan persons were killed on Monday evening by an expo- don of gad which occurred in a large tunnel in process of con- struction under Lake Brie in connection with the water works there. A rescue pgrty penetrated for a distance of about 5,00011.. but were compelled to return. They found the bottom of the tunnel covered with a pocallar substanie resembling snow. A light boat to'. transport to Klondyke has recently boon built at White's shipyard, Olagow. It 13 entirely of aluminium. Including plates angles, and rivets. Although 18ft. long, it scales only a little more than 2cwt. It is built In sections ready for putting together after arrival at the overland teminus, and is so compact that a small boa will contain it. A correspondent of the "Field "tells of a struggle between a cuckoo and a pied wagtaii. The former laid its egg on an asphalte path and carried it up in its bill to the nest of the wagtail. The wagtail resented this unwarrantable intrusion, and there was a set-to. Ultimately one of the wagtail's eggs was smashed and the bird driven off by the cu-dcoo, which placed its egg safely in the nest. Mr. Thomas Owen, M.P. owner of the " Western Dail Mercury " and other Plymouth newspapers has met h,s death under sad circumstances at ho Welch home near Machynlieth While taking a walk on Sunday night he slipped over a precipice into a stream and was drowned. At the inquest on Monday a verdict of "Accidental death " was returned, The camp of the National Rifle Assoliation at Sisley opened on Monday for the reception of the voluntevs and otheetrig snw who are to take part lathe annual competitions The meeting this year shows slight falling off in regard to the number of entries in the principal Competitions compared with last year, when an added interest was given to the event by the presence of the colonial visitors in celebration 0 the Queen's Jubilee,

• Joseph Whyte, engine-driver, residing in Bury. Wal in- dicted at Manchester AftiliZei on Wednesday for having caused the death of William Alfred Hicklia and Ellen The prisoner was driver of a train from Morecambe which overran the signals at Leyland Station on Whit Thursday and ran into a train from Blackpool. The jury found the prisoner guilty, but with a recommendation to mercy, and he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. Experiments In wireless telegraphy are in progress under newspaper auspices by Mr. C. Dottamr, son of Prof. Dolbear, and messages, it appears, have thus far been succeasfully transmitted over a distanee of some 1,600 feet. Prof. Slaby has also devoted some attention to the subject, and is said to have sent intelligible Morse signals thirteen and a quarter miles, using two balloons filed with hydrogen to elevate the ends of the conductors to the height of one thousand feat in the air. At a meeting of the South-east Lancashire district fifths National Union of Teachers held in Manch 'stet on Saturday, , a letter was read from the Bi,hon of Hereford on the subject of "equal financial support" torahl schools, Board and Vol- untary. Dr. Percival pointed out that the Voluntary s.thoois have little chance of doing as good work for their children as the Board schools have unless porno plan can be devised by which they would receive equal financial support. But justice and nubile sentiment, the Bishop added, required that it the Voluntary schools were to be thus supported by public money they must be under public and not private manage- ment.

The instructions given to Sir D. P, Chalmers, the Corn- mi4sioner appointed to incinie inta the native insurrection in Sierra Leone and, the general affairs of the colony and pro- tectorate state that It has been alleged that the insurrection at its commencement was caused by the imposition ol a hut tax and by the steps taken to enforce its collection. The Commissioner is to inquire into the tmuth of these statements and particularly to Inluire whether in the circumstances of the Protectorate it was neceasary or expedient to impose the tax, whether the amount Wm unnecesswily high, whether the mode of enforcing its payment provided by the law was suitab!e, and whether the collection of the tax and the enforcement of its payment were properly carried out by tbe officers and others entrusted with this cllty.

div.head: EXAMINER. FRIDNY„TULY 15, 1b98:
div.p: THE EXAMINER. FRIDNY„TULY 15, 1b98:

an excellent way. It was their imperative duty to be and do something in this mighty cause. (Applause.) The Rev. Ef ..T. Tereoa said he regretted that these speeches had not been delivered first in the House of Commons, and repeated in ~he House of Lords. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Herbert Gladstone ought to have heard them, Sir William Adams,the weak-kneed and defeated candidate for West Staff md,and the Liberals of the city of Durham ought to have heard them. They had prisons, poorhouses, and public-houses in abundance, but how many more would they have had had it not been for the 50 years of this movement ? (Applause). It was per- fectly true that the whale sentiment of England had been changed on the temperance question during the last 0 years. They could not find one doctor or one saes man from Land's End to John O'Groats' who would undertake to say that alcohol was necessary for the support of health. Find such a man and take him to Barnum and Bailey's show, and they would get £l,OO for him as one of the greatest curiosities on earth. (Laughter.) Already there were four millions of adult abstainer', and these would be reinforced by thousands of temperance people ia this country, who would in the v4ry near future gather in the harvest of Sunday closing for England. (Applause.) The movement would soon be reinforced by three mil- lions of boys and girls, and when the next century was but young this democratic army of seven or eight mil- lions strong in these democratic times would call to the ' bar of conscience, of marina and of righteousness all the men and women who had by their efforts and indiffer- ence aelayed the ingathering of the temperancb harvest. They would rise and demand that certain things should come to pass, and as sure as the next century would come they would curse these who for the sake of ten per cent. tools shares in breweries.—(Hear, hear.) This army of sane and sober men and women would call brewers moral exotics, and the money made in that traffic would be refused by all Christians. (Applause.) Christian men and women would in the near future call to acccunt those officials of Christian churches who Pro- viand intoxicating drink for the Lord's Supper. The Band of Haps boys and girls would say in the near future that the working men should have the same right to protect themselves against the presence of public. houses in their midst as the ground landlord had. They would have no quarter for any Government that left this questieu alone, anti they would make short work of any Government that merely appointed a commission to sit on ergs that they did not want to hatch. (Hear, I bear, and Is ughter.) The day was coming when neither Herbert Glaastone,nor the petty be represented, nor any I other party could ill afford to drop this question. By dropping this qeestion they would be dropping the most sane and golly men and women of the country. There was growing up in England an irresistible force, which was time force of Tootle E eland on the side of temper- ance and righteeuseess and God, and all the licences and present evils of the licensing laws would vanish. If they were prepared to do their best in their day and generation those who came after them would see that th:s England of ours was swept from the evil of intoxi- cating drinks. (Applause.) During the evening musical items were agreeably in- terspersed by the choir, and Miss Hettie Maw Isley was encored for her fine sslo singing. The services of the Chairman and speakers were acknowledged on the pro- position of the Rev. E. T. Reed, seconded by the Rev. W. H. Drummond.

div.head: LANCASHIRE AND CaESHIRE BAND OF , HOPE AND TEMPERANCE UNION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE AND CaESHIRE BAND OF , HOPE AND TEMPERANCE UNION.
MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.

In Parr Hall, Warrington, on Saturday, the executive meetings in connection with the above mentioned union were lield,and were well attended. The delegates and those taking part in the proceed- ings numbered 250, and prior to the public confer- ence which was held in the afternoon, the party was photographed by Mr. Parkinson, of Sankey- street. Excellent arrangements had been made for the meetings by Mr. W. Chandos Wilson (Counties Union secretary), and Mr. E. Lloyd Jones (secretary Warrington and District Band of Hope Union). It will perhaps be remembered that a few months ago ' a meeting was held in the Lecture Room at the Y.M.C.A. Rooms when it was decided by the representatives of the Warrington Bands of Hope to join the Union under whose auspices the meetings were held on Satur- day. In the thirty-fourth annual report for the year ending December 31st last, some interesting particulars are given of the work that is being car- ried on by the Union. It appears that early is the year, the Committee arranged to heartily co-operate with the United Kingdom Band of Hope Union in carrying out their proposals for celebrating the Jubilee of the Movement, of which the following were the principal : "To secure in the United Kingdom, during the year, 1,000,000 more members largely through visitation of homes ; to extend the scientific day school lecture scheme, by the engage- ment of additional lecturers ;to institute temper- ance work in all villages, by the engagement of special village lecturers ; to arrange for thanksgiv- ing services in all churches and Sunday schools; to arrange for public demonstrations in all towns in the United Kingdom; to raise a national fund of £24,000, and a counties fund of £6,000 for Lanca- shire and Cheshire, to be chiefly devote,' to the extension of Day School Scientific Lectares." Con- ferences were held with the local Unions, leading temperance and philantropic friends,in many owns and Jubilee committees started, acting in conjunc- tion with the Counties Union's Committee, to carry out the various proposals. In several places Jubilee funds were started on behalf of the local as well as the Counties efforts. "In every Case," continues the report "where this Jubilee effort was under- taken it was found that not only were additional interest created, and greater ',influence secured, but the ordinary work was greatly benefited." The report proceeds to state how the various phases of the scheme were carried out.ffender the heading of the strength of the Union toe report states that " During the year, in addi- tion tgandlas part of the Jubilee effort much attention was given to the organisation of the movement. The result has been that many new Bands of Hope have been started the Erstwhile flagging Baud of Hope,lUnions in Church and Oswaldwistle, Colne, Eccles, Hollinwood, North wich, Royton, and Salford and Wigan have been revived, New Bend of Hope Unions have been formed for the first time in Hoylake and West Kirby, Trawden and the vigor- ous Unions of Nelson, New Mills, and tho South Lancashire federation of branches of the Young Abstainers' Union have been brought into direct association with the Counties Union, which is stronger to-day and more influential than ever be- fore. The present strength of the Union is 73 town or district Unions, comprising 1,360 secietiers, with a total membership of 214,464. a net advance of 4 unions, 117 societies, and 14,970 members." THE AFTERNOON PROCEEDINGS._

of another agent ought to be secured. Whenever a sufficient number of societies was found in a giv district a local union ought to be formed. They ought not to have societies holding aloof and work- ing in an isolated manner. The chief hindrance to county work had all along been the pecuniary diffi- culties of the parent union. If the work of the future was to be done efficiently the income of the Union must be larger and permanently increased. In conclusion he said they must be determined that the whole of the two counties should be thor- oughly miesi mad until every town and district should have its union end every Sabbath school ita Band of Hope Society. An interesting discussion followed the reading of the paper. Mr. Henry Thornton was the first ept akar. He expressed the opinion that in War- rington they had been very much behind in Band of Hope work. He thought much could be done by temperance workers going to the parents of child- ren, and showing them the advantages of temper- ance. He also advocated a freer use of the pledge card, and let it be a card which the owner would think something of and appreciate. Amongst the other speakers was the Rev E. T. Reed, of the Emmanuel Reformed Church of England. He said there had been a distinct departure in some Bands of Hooe from the right way of conducting them. The entertainment part had been allowed to over- lap the educational part, and it seemed to him that if their Band of Hope workers saw the necessity of giving temperance teaching on every occasion it would help their Band of Elope work. Re proceeded to refer to an incident he witnessed in Canada, of the presentation of a petition to the Premier of Canada by Temperanco women. The petition was presented by a lady wtio was a prominent temperance worker, and whom he afterwards learned, was first enrolled under the banner of temperance at a Ssnd of Hope meeting. Be thought that wee a beautiful trophy to the work of the Band of Hope.—Verioue sug.psations were mule by other speakers for extending the work of the Band of Hope movement, including the more extended use of cyclists in Band of Hope work in the c nintry villages. A vote of thanks was passed to the Cnairm in and Mr. Hallawarth on the proposition of the Rev. (Idealise Piach, seconded by lir. William Roberts.

At the couclu—s-ic-m—Of the clnferance, the delegates were eater.ained to tea in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom by Hr. R A. Naylor. After an excel- lent repast. Mr. and Miss Naylor's hospitality and kindness was acknowledged on the proposition of the Rev. Canon Flicks—Mr. Naylor and Miss Naylor suitably replied.

THE PUBLIC MEETING. In the evening a great public festival was held in Parr Hall under the presidency of Mr. R. A. N.aylor. special music was rendered by the War- rington Bind of Elope Union Choir of 350 voices, assisted by members of the Manchester District Band of Hope Choral Union. The choir was under the conductorship of Mr. W. Brough, and the accompaniments were played by Mr. Wilkes, A.L..0.11. (organist), and Mrs. Heaton. The onerous duties of secretary to the choir were discharged by Mr. Wood. At 630 a special musical programme was commenced including choruses by the Man- chester Choral Union and the Warrington United choir, and an organ selection by Mr. Wilkes. The performances were highly creditable, and the audience showed their approval by hearty applause At seven o'clock the meetisg commenced by the winging of the hymn " Soldiers of Christ." Mr. Naylor was supported on the platform by Miss Naylor, Miss Bessie Dutton. the Rev. Canon Hicks (Manchester),the Rev.H.J. Taylor (Southport), Rev. C.Finch, Mr. H. Thornton, Mr. William Roberts, Mr. E. Lloyd-Jonw,Mr. Chandos Wilson,Mr. Hallsworth, and others.

The Cuaram.sx, in opening the pr)ceedings, said he was very [leased to sea such a large assembly. lie was not so enamoured of large gatherings because they had had them before in Warrington, and g3nerally speaking they had ended in smoke. In this union, just estab- lished under such favourable auspices, they must re- member one thinr,that when they wont away from that large gathering the work still wanted doing. (sear, bear.) The work moat be done by individual effort and alsiatance. If they were to get a batter state of things in this drunken cmittry they must work week by week. month by month, and year by year, and keep pegging away until the work waa accomplished. Be made those few observations with the idoa that he might encourage them to put their shoulders to the wheel ,and work for the end they had in view. (Applause.) _ .

The Rev. CANON Elmo said he attended that meeting with very great interest as he was present at a meeting In Warrington only a few weeks ago at which a number of friends gathered together in order to form a Band of Hope Union for Warringtoa. He was very thankful that that Band of Hope Union was formed, and out of its formation had come that interesting gathering in which they joined that day. (Applause). As President of the Lancashire and Cheshire Ueion, he wished to thank the Warrington people very warmly for the splendid reception the visitors had received throughout the day (Hear, hear.) The Chairman had spoken to them what he called words of encouragement. It was quite true that they needed encouragement. Oa looking back half a century they could easily see what rapid strides the temperance movement had image. But there still remained a large amount of work yet to be done; and while temperance work advanced and temperance agitation spread, what were the consequences ? W hy, it was this, that the public opinion of the country was becoming so consoli- dated on the temperance side, that hardly a bench of magistrates could be found that dare give a new license. (Bear, hear.) Whilst the temperance opinion of the country had been consolidated, the drink-sellers and the drink interest had also been consolidated to a degree that , history had never yet known. The consequence was,that whilst they had temperance literature, the brewers were also distributing literature. Messrs. Walker, the well- known brewers, of Liverpool, issued a pamphlet broad- cast over the country in order to prove that temperance workers were in the wrong, and that the progress and advance and well-being of the country was due to Pro. per indulgence in strong drink of all kinds. (Leug iter.) They had come to a crisis in which on the one side they had the growth and consolidation of temperance oPird°l3 and on the other side they were confronted by the whole and consolidated interest of this great and he was going to say iniquitous traffic. (Applause.) The oppos- ing forces were drawing nearer and nesrer, and in the near future they would require all the help they could get in carrying out this great coellect to the eod,and he thanked God that they had a large army of children as recruits. When he went to a temperance meeting he saw all ages represented,but he generally found—and it was a most important fact—that the majority were of younger age. The forces of temperance would be larger in the future than to-day. (Hear, hear). Referring to the leakage from temperance societies, the Canon said their bends of hope did not remain as large as they ought to do, and if they were not recruited by new members the leakage would seem larger than it reallY was WhY, he asked, was there any leakage from their bands of hope ? One reason was beaause they as tem- perance workers did not really teach their young people with that precision they should do in tha bands of hoPe. Then there was another fault, which was, that they did not read and study the subject sufficiently. They did not sufficiently teach themselves beforehand. Then there were some of their young people who became too proud to be taught at all. If they saw them smoking and courting they would think it a wonder how it all hap pened. One of the remedies for the leakage would be to draft the young folks connected with the band of hope societies, into the great temperance benefit societies. It would not only connect them with an extremely good benefit society,but one that woul I never meet in a public- house. That was one way to prevent the leakage. Then he night also ask why dide't they use the young People for open-air and other kinds of work. He thought they ought to train up the young folks for the work. Let them apprentice the young to all kinds of Christian and temperance work. He appealed to his hearers to set themselves the task, and they would be proud that they bad raised up a band of workers to take their places when God called them away. If they did this they would stop the leakage of which they complained. They must train them up, not to be workers only, but also to be fightera. They must be fighters and workers all along. Whilst he (Canon Hicks) was on the watch he would follow his leaders, namely. the Archbishop of Canterbury, Sir Wilfred Lawson, and others. He would follow them, for he had got his sword at his side, and would vote or speak in order to fight against that which was after all the greet source of leakage—he meant the awful and excessive temptations that bound their young on every side. If they worked in this spirit and practi- cal method ho was quite sure that there need be no fear of the results. (Loud applause). Miss BESSIE Derron at the outset of an interesting address defended the British Women's Temperance Association, referring to some of the Chairman's remarks concerning it which were not very complimen- tary. She proceeded to refer to the difficalty of temper- ance work amongst children. They had to contend against hereditary circumstances, and also their present surroundings and circumstances. All children liked the taste of alcohol. The youngest child would greedily suck alcoholic drink. In a recent medical discussion on the subjeet of alcoholism a Dublin doctor spoke of a case of a child, eight sears of age, who had been treated in a Dublin hospital suffering from delirium tremens. It appeared that the child, who had a drunken mother, one day discovered a bottle of wine, and before it was seen he had consumed all but a little. This was the begin- ning of the delirium tremens, and the child was in the hospital from January to April before it could be cured. She urged temperance workers to foster the other side of a child's nature which was susceptible to teaching. Teetotalers were not always Chrietians,but they were on

The Rev. Canon limes, president of the Union, occupied the chair at the conterence when Mr. T. E. Hallsworth (hon. secretary of the Counties Union) read a paper prefatory to a discassion on the sub- ject: "The Baud of Hope Jubilee and the responsi- bilities it has brought us." In the course of his paper Mr. Halisworth traced the history of the Band of Hope movement,and stated that at the Ju- bilee celebrations of the Band of Hope last year there were 22,188 Bands of Hope with 3,025,410 in the United Kingdom. The strength of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union at the beeinning of the year stood at 1,360 societies and 214,464 members. Since then it had been greatly increiseed. Tole was very encoaragine and they all felt ready to exclaim " We will thank God and take courage." But the Jubilee figures not only revealed to them what had been accomplished but they showed to them how much re- mained to be done before all the children were safeguarded within the Bands of Hope. While there were now about 3i millions of children in their societies there must be at least seven million more children of school age who were outside, and who but for their mag- nificent day school scheme would not come under temperance teaching at all. This teaching,however, was only administered once or twice a year and therefore strenuous efforts must be put forth to Rather the children in. This then was one of the greatest of the responsibilities that now came to them. Although they had 214,464 members in Lancashire and Cheshire they had nearly one mil- lion children of school age and about 800,000 of all ages in the Sabbath schools. He wished they could impress unpon that important gathering the neces- sity for accepting the responsibility placed open them and for resolutely facing chi difficulties in the way. They must give their atten- tion more earnestly to the question of retaining the members they had got. The Jubilee returns shewed a large accession of new members obtained by the " million more scheme" and their last report showed an increase of 14,970 members, but it would be exceedingly interesting to know how many young people returned as members the pre- vious year had ceased to be such at the end of the twelve months following. He ventured to sug- gest that they would be startled if they had these figures before theme shewing how many had liter- lully passed through their Banes of Hope. Where to? Why out into the world to be exposed to all the dangers and snares and temptations of the terrible traffic, without the safeguard of the mem- bership and teaching of their movement. The responsibility of checking in seine measure this terrible leakage rested on them. How was it to be done? Not by mere entertainment. (Hear, bear.) The world to-day was offering this tar better and with more enticing surroundings. Entertain- ment they must have but let them see to it that it was pure and elevating and not an imitation and a poor one at that of what was given in the music ball. Special attention must also be paid to the character of the advocacy at Band of Hope meet- ings. They must have less of the declamatory and sensational and more ot the teaching element. Greater use must be made of the blackboard, the Idiagrams and the scientific experiment, so that their young people might be fully equipped against the time when they left their societies. More literature must be circulated and a more general 1190 made of the requisites of the " Onward office" and other publishers— such as pledge cards, hymn books,recitation books etc. To maintain the extention and consolidation work conferences of workers must be held with more frequency so that the interest might be thoroughly awakened and maintained. The en- thusiasm enkindled by the Jubilee celebrations must not be allowed to die out. Every assistance in this direction was cheerfully and efficiently ren- dered by their indefatigable secretary, Mr. Wilson, Their great day school scheme must be maintained at any cost for by this means alone could they hope to reach the children whom they failed to get into their bands of hope. The work of forming new societies and of establishing new unions must be taken in hand vigorously. The interesting maps drawn by Mr. Wilaou revealed that there were still many centres ill the two counties, and notably the village distincts to which much attention needed to be given if they were to be in all parts thoroughly won for the Band of Hope movement. They must aim at securing a complete network of Bands of Hops and locil unions spread over the two countries,and in doing BO the rural districts must have early consideration. The Sunday schoola must be visited and the managers induced to start Bands of Hope. The nearest local union might render good service in this work, but he believed that to do it thoroughly end efficiently the RervlcPs makamaimaimilaindeif

FARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
MUSICAL.

At the examination held at Liverpool on July 2nd in connection with Trinity College, London,the tollowing cundidates were successful in pianoforte playing Miis Mabel Mitchell and Master Fred Pick- up. Both are pupils of Miss L. Bailey,l22, Market- street, Earlestown. DEUNKIINNEEIS.

At the Earlestovrn Police Station on Monday morning before Mr. J. W. Emmett, John Kelly, Athol-street, Earlestown : Miles Platting of Hay- dock, and Charles Watson were each fined 2s. Gd. and costs for being drunk. Kelly in Earlestown on Saturday, Platting at Newton, and Watson on Sun- day. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SIINDAY SCHOOL.

The annual treat to the scholars attending the above school took place on Tuesday afternoon. The children assembled at the school shortly after one o'clock,and marched in procession to a &ild off Ash- ton-lane,kindly lent by Mr. W. Longton. On arri- val they dispersed to amuse themselves in various ways, and about four o'clock buns and milk were served out. After the tea, racing and games occu- pied the remainder of the evening until dusk, when the tired youngsters dispersed to their homes.

CoLLI&R'S EXCUIVION Flaws COLLINS GREEN. The annual excursion in connection with the em- ployes of the Collins Green Colliery, took place on Saturday afternoon,to Blackpool, Two trains con- veying about 1,800 colliers and their families left Collins Green at 545 and 5.55, arriving at Black- pool shortly after seven o'clock. The day was beautifully fine,lnd every opportunity was given to trippers to visit the various entertainments, whilst many spent a day on the beach. Blackpool was left behind about 10 o'clock and home was reached about midnight.

E. Weeks, Stage 2, 2nd ; M. A. Davies, A. Eaton, A. R. Hill, J. El. Latbam, May Sweetlove, Stage 1. 2nd. Machine Construction :—W. U. Beilby, let A ; W. Bailiff, James Burgess. Rayer, 2nd E. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. The annual fl)vver service held in aid of the treat to the scholars attending the Sunday school con- nected with the above church,took place on Sunday. The morning service was conducted by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar, and the evening, by the Rev. Mr. Wolkenberg, of Ashton, both of whom preached appropriate sermons. A children's service was hold in the afternoon,when bunches of beautiful flowers wPre presented by the children, and a suitable dis- course was given by the Rev. F. C. Shirtcliffe (curate). On Monday the flowers were despatched to the Warrington Infirmary,Warrington Union,and to some of the sick people in the parish.

. . GOOD TEMPLAARS AT ASIITON•IN-MAKBRFIELD. The monthly meeting of the 1.0.G.T. No. 1 Con- vention S.W. Lancashire was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Warrington-road, Ashton-in- Makerfield, on Saturday. Bro. 'I aylor, C Co., pre- sided, and there was a good muster of representa- tives from Warrington, Leigh, Wigan, Earlestown. Haydock, Ashton, Sutton, Se Helene, and Widnes. The Press and Credential Committees were ap- pointed, after which Bro. Lodge C. Secretary, pre- sented a satisfactory report, The Executive Com- mittee's report was afterwards presented. The lodge and juvenile representatives gave reports of the working of various lodeee and temples. The Convention decided to hold the August session at t. Helens. At the close of the meeting tea was provided by the Ashton members, t, whom a vote of thanks was given. Elitratarows CONSERVAT/YD CLUB. The annual picnic in connection with the Earles- town Conservative Club took place on Saturday afternoon: About 90 members and friends left the Club premises in wagonettes at 1-15, and driving by way oh Collins Green, Bold, and Farnworth, arrived at Hale after about l hours pleasant drive. The Wellington Hotel was made the headquarters of the party, and arrangements having been made for an inspection of the grounds attached to Hale Hall the residence of Colonel Blackburne, the privi- lege was taken full advantage of,the stroll through the spacious grounds being thoroughly enjoyed. A substantial tea was partaken of at about 4 o clock. The weather was beautifully fine, and the outing was much enjoyed,Earlestown being reached in the ao•ning rahnrtly hufara 10 &plebe',

Sr. HELENS COUNTY . LICENSING SESSIONS.

Petty Sessions, On Tuesday. at the SG. Helens Count the magistrates (Messrs. H. Martin and J. Bs,echam) ap- pointed Wednesday, the 7th September, as the general annual licensing day for the St. Helens petty sessional district. The Mayor (Lieutenant-Colonel R. Pilkington) was appointed the district representative on the county licensing committee.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT A ST. HELENS GLASSWORKS. Samuel Eccleston, 19 years of age, a glass beveltar, of 46, Corporation-street, St. Helens, died on Tuosday,from injuries received at Messrs. Pilkington's Plate Glass Works on Monday. He was working at one of the be- velling machines, when a large piece of glass flew off and caught him in tie stomach. THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT Sr. HELENS.

John Green, of 12, Phythian-street, appeared at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, on the adjourned charge of attempted suicide. Chief Constable Wood said that the man and his wife bad been separated, and after drinking for some days Green jumped into the canal,but was rescued by a man named Macdonald. He had been at Walton Gaol for seven days, and now promised not to do anything of the sort again. His wife said she would go badk to live with him, and there was every prospect that Green would reform.—On promising to keep the pledge Green was discharged.
SINGULAR CHARGE OF HIGHWAY RORIIRRY..

On Monday morning at the St. Helens Police Court, Thomas Critchley (Watson-street). Michael Fallon (21, Stanley-street), John M'Gunnigle (6, Cyril-strest).James Owen (Ti, Cyril-street), and John W. Thompson(Bound- ary-road) were charged with stealing 4s: 61., with vio- lence from John Tobin, a glass-bender,of 38,Cyril-street, on Sunday night. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the prisoners, who pleaded not guilty.—lt appeared that late on Sunday night the prosecutor saw the prisoners near Cyril-street, and had an argument with them as t* the "singing" or whistling abilities of a canary. The conversation ended in a bet of 61. with one of the men, and it was alleged that the prisoners ultimately seized prosecutor and forcibly took the amount named from his pockets. The prosecutor admitted that he was drunk at the time, and could not say which of the men took the money from him. The bench dismissed the case without hearing the defence. SCENE LT A ST. HELENS PIIBLIC-HOUSE.

- - Lawrence Wheelan, labourer, of 25, Back Appleton- street, was charged at St. Helens, on Monday, with being drunk and assaulting Constable Littler, and also with doing wilful damage to a spirit keg, a decanter, a syphon, and other articles, to the amount of £3, at the New Vaults Inn, Peasley Cross-lane, the property of James Moyers.—Mr. E. W. Swift prosecuted, and said that on Saturday night about half-past nine o'clock Wheelan went into the Now Vaults and asked for drink. As he was drunk Miss Moyers refused to serve him. Thereupon Wheelan threw a ing across the bar at Miss Moyers,and it struck a decanter of brandy and smashed it. lie then threw a sodawo.ter syphon and smashed a spirit keg and a number of other articles. The police were sent for, and Constant° Littler took Wheelan into custody. The uproar was not yet put an end to, as Wheelan threw himself down and kicked the officer severely, saying that he wanted to disfigure him for life. —Prisoner said that all Miss Moyers said was true. He was drunk at the time. He was fined £2 damages, 6cl. fine and 4.3. CO'itS, or a month, and 533. and 4s. or seven , days for the kirutilrenness.

THE OUTBREAK OF YELLOW FEVER. MADRID, TianasnaY. The Minister of Foreign Affairs state that p'aog negotiations have not yet taken place, but that the, representations attributed to the Ambassador of one of the Great Powers are of a semi-official character. Marshal Blanco is reported to have telegraphed General Toral calling upon him to resist the AtHOTiRAOB." WASHINGTON, rIXTIRSDAT. The worst news is the heal,h of the troops. TIIB dreaded " yellow Jack "has broken out at last. Alreadl there are cases certifi-d from the regiments actually ott- the front attacking line. Previously there had been lon'l fevers of a few day's duration, followed by apparent.] recovery. Every possible precaution has been taken 1511 the medical staff, but apparently the germs of the, disease have been too many for the rhea red kicNi by cow' liaual hardship and the earlier fever. Mr. W.Kinley determined that every possible resource be furnished te the hospital staff. A special isolated hospital will be established at once.

REPORTED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF MARSITAL BLANCO. A Cuban reports that Marshal Blanco attempted suicide when he learned the fate of Admiral Cervera's fiset,and that he was closeted with the staff and General Arolas at the time. After a struggle he was disarmed, and subdued. The shock was so swoere that the Governor-General was compdled to remain in bed for three days. The story is hos confir ned from any other source.
